title: Roadmap
section: Done since: absence, schools and twins
text:
Done since: absence, schools and twins

What goes with school absence. A page that starts from a map of the UK research (with links to the sources), shows the trend by reason since 2016/17, and models seven kinds of absence in 2025/26 on every secondary school’s intake, needs and setting, with each school nested in its authority and region. Shapley shares say how much each group of characteristics explains, and the full models (coefficients, random effects, fit) are on the page.
The school’s part. What the models attribute to “the school” is mostly selection through admissions; what is left between similar schools is wide and lasts from one year to the next. A message for heads and governors, nationally and on every area page.
Absence on every Sussex page. Each authority’s and district’s absence against England, its neighbours and the tier above, what in its intake raises or lowers it, and its schools against similar schools in both years.
Find a twin. Choose a school and find the schools in England most like it in intake and setting, or the look-alikes that do better on absence, attainment or value added, on a chart and a map, with fact cards side by side. Linked from the absence page and every area page, and every comparison has its own link.
How school absence changes (started). Every secondary school followed from 2016/17 to 2025/26 through academy conversion and changes of trust: what is lasting and what moves, whether schools keep their place, who rose most since the pandemic, whether absence moves when a school’s own intake does, and event studies of becoming an academy and of a change of trust.
The explorer. Ofsted colours that work across both inspection regimes, in each palette, and the spread of schools on the map beneath it, as on the Sussex pages.

title: Roadmap
text:
Next

Policy simulator v2.0. The Pull the Right Lever simulator rebuilt on the v2.1 models, in the browser: absence and the intake terms as levers (with admissions and sixth form for one school), all five groups at once with the disadvantage gap, each lever’s contribution, and an area mode that applies a change to every school in a district, authority, region or England.
Adding a new year. When DfE publishes a new year’s KS4 results, add it to YEAR_CONFIG in pipeline/helpers.R, run R/00_fetch_data.R, then the build steps. The v2.1 model takes its years from the data, and no longer needs the workforce file, which was the slowest to arrive. See the README.
A self-contained data pipeline for the model. R/00_fetch_data.R builds every model input from public sources (DfE, GIAS, ONS, nomis, postcodes.io, Ofsted), with the scripts in pipeline/. Rebuilt from the same downloads it reproduces the inputs, and every value-added figure, exactly.
The Sussex area analyses, self-contained too. The area pages still reuse the original project’s area analyses (a snapshot in data/area/), its Sussex governance and its absence reasons. Port its R/15, R/17 and R/19 next.
Update 2025/26 with the revised KS4 release (February 2027). 2025/26 is shown now, provisional, predicted from the fitted model on DfE’s October results with absence bridged and the unpublished intake data carried forward (R/05_provisional_2526.R). Rerun it on the revised results; then, once the year’s census, SEN and mobility data are out, fold 2025/26 into the model as a fifth year.
v2.1 candidates tested across every group: the illness share of absence and an 11–16 flag (the methodology), with a chart of what matters most in the model.
v2.1 published. The 11–16 flag is in the expectation (a school’s structure, like its admissions policy). Value added allowing for the kind of absence is published beside it, not in it, because what is authorised as illness is partly a school’s own coding.
Neighbourhood types (OAC). The 2021/2 Output Area Classification profiled over each school’s 150 nearest Output Areas at all three tiers. It reproduces neighbourhood education, adds nothing to results or to value added within authorities, and describes the places behind the authority effects for disadvantaged pupils (multicultural urban areas above, small-town, coastal and former industrial areas below). Groups are enough; subgroups add little.
Geographical effects across England. How much of value added is region and local authority, for every group; a map of the authority effects; region averages; and what goes with them.
Neighbourhood covariates (experiment). Ten Census 2021 measures and each school’s own White British share added to v2.1. For disadvantaged pupils, the ethnic pattern is mostly composition (pupils, not place); neighbourhood deprivation beyond qualifications is place. Together they take about a fifth off the authority effects and over a third off the regional ones for disadvantaged pupils; about a third of Brighton and Hove’s effect.
v2.2 candidates tested across every group and year. Neighbourhood household deprivation helps every group in every year (recommended for v2.2). Pupils’ ethnicity (school White British share, each January) matters almost only for disadvantaged pupils, where it is large; recommended beside the headline, not in it.
Value Added v2.2 (agreed, for a future release). The approach from the v2.2 candidates is agreed but not yet built: refit every group with neighbourhood household deprivation in the expectation beside neighbourhood education; publish value added allowing for pupils’ ethnicity beside the headline, labelled, not in it; and before release, test detailed ethnic groups rather than the White British share alone. Until then the site publishes v2.1.
Parents, not adults. Neighbourhood education rebuilt from custom Census tables as graduates among parents (adults 25-64 with dependent children, MSOA). All-adult graduate shares hide a 12-point gap in parents between deprived and comfortable graduate-rich neighbourhoods, and the young-adult penalty almost disappears. Parents alone is no better a term; parents and other adults together help every group a little. Deprivation survives.
v2.2 candidate: split neighbourhood education into parents and other adults, and follow up why disadvantaged pupils do better near graduates without children.
What causes school-level absence, continued. The cross-section and change over time are under way (above). Next: each school’s own path relative to England on the area pages and in Find a twin, whether high-illness places such as Brighton and Hove record absence differently, the severe tail on its own, whether particular trusts’ schools move together, and absence against intake by kind as a candidate for a future version of the model.
Twins, further. The matching is weighted by what matters for the measure chosen (equal weights still available), the fact cards show value added and absence year by year against the twin and England, and a comparison prints cleanly for a governors’ meeting.
Distance to school: the straight-line check. The distance from every neighbourhood in England to its nearest state secondary, by deprivation, in every district and authority. Across England deprived neighbourhoods are usually nearer; in Brighton and Hove they are about a third further away. Absence goes with distance by authority, more for disadvantaged pupils, and by school, mostly in illness and persistent absence. It builds on FFT Education Datalab’s finding that pupils who live further away are absent more often.
How firm is the link with absence? Six years, eleven measures of distance and thousands of models for all three groups of pupils, a falsification test on primary absence, DfE’s absence by home neighbourhood within each authority, and changes in the school network. The link is consistent and stronger for disadvantaged pupils, but most of its size between authorities is ethnic mix; a smaller link remains in towns and cities, within authorities and between schools. Every source and calculation is in the methodology.
Journey times on the real networks. Walking and bus times with r5r from every Output Area in Brighton and Hove and eight comparator places, with changes of bus, the penalty for missing a journey, school buses and the climb each way. Brighton and Hove stands out on real journeys as it does in straight lines. None of these shows a clear general link with absence yet; Longhill stands out on missing the bus.
Journey times for the 109 mostly urban authorities. Every Output Area routed on 28 networks, London included (buses only). No authority’s deprived neighbourhoods are as far from a school as Brighton and Hove’s, mostly because of distance, and they need the most changes of bus. Time does not beat straight-line distance for absence, and changes, waits and missing a bus add nothing once distance is known. The climb is the one feature that keeps appearing.
Points of interest around bus changes and along walking routes. From OpenStreetMap, in five groups. Nothing across authorities; within authorities a hint that busier change points go with more secondary absence, mostly in London, where bus-only routes are least like real journeys.
What it could mean for GCSE results. Distance carried through absence to Attainment 8, a direct check, and Gorard and Siddiqui’s mixing estimate on the same scale.
What Brighton and Hove’s admissions changes did. From the city’s school system model: the 2024 map and priority 6 lengthened disadvantaged children’s journeys by well under a minute and lowered segregation a little. Both are worth a fraction of an Attainment 8 point; where the schools are matters far more.
The proposals that did not go ahead. The council’s 2024 proposal (priority 6 at 20%, Stringer and Blatchington Mill at 300) and priority 6 at 30%, run on the published model: longer journeys and more children displaced, no gain in mixing, and nothing more from 30% than from 20%.
Rail, Metro and trams. Timetables beyond the Bus Open Data Service, for London and the large conurbations.
School bells. Published start times for each school, in place of the time inferred from the last school bus, for the penalty for missing one.
Distance to school: how far each school’s pupils travel. A better measure than each school’s nearest children, such as a gravity model of who goes where, built from published sources.
Distance to school: does it matter more in towns and cities? The hypothesis: distance matters for attendance more than is understood, and may matter more in towns and cities, where a longer journey passes more places to stop on the way (intervening opportunities), than in rural areas, where long journeys are the norm and often by school transport. Between authorities the link is strong in mostly urban places and absent in less urban ones, but within authorities and by school it is similar in both, so it needs journey times and data on school transport.
Independent schools. What is published for them, term by term against v2.1; why their Attainment 8 cannot be compared (IGCSEs score nothing, and KS4 and A level results are unrelated); a test showing a reduced specification gets value added badly wrong even in the state sector; and the comparison that does exist, DfE’s A level value added. Verdict: no value added at 16 is possible from published data.
Independent schools: IGCSEs. DfE’s 16-19 guidance checked: A level value added counts approved GCSEs only, so IGCSEs are left out of the baseline (most independent students still have some GCSEs). Attainment 8 completed from its published parts: the average grade in counting GCSEs, validated on state schools (R² 0.88-0.90) and against independent schools’ own A level results (r 0.84, against 0.03).
Independent schools, next. A level value added over three years and by subject; the completed Attainment 8 over several years; and the two sectors’ sixth forms side by side by area.
Areas beyond Sussex. The area template works for any authority and its districts once boundaries are added.
Monthly Ofsted refresh. A GitHub Actions workflow picks up Ofsted’s new release on the 20th of each month, updates every school’s latest judgement without refitting, rerenders and commits.
Publish v2.1 alongside v1 in the original reports, labelled, with a note on how rankings change.

title: West Sussex
text:
What goes with absence here
The national absence analysis models seven kinds of absence in every secondary school in England, using autumn and spring 2025/26 and the January 2026 census. Here it is applied to West Sussex’s 38 schools with full data. It compares them with England, with Sussex, the South East, East Sussex and Brighton and Hove.








Figure 12: Absence in West Sussex and its comparators against England’s average school, autumn and spring 2025/26. Hollow, the whole difference; filled, the part the schools’ intake, needs and setting do not account for (the national models’ region, authority and school effects). Schools in brackets.






Overall, West Sussex’s schools have 3% more absence than England’s average school. Once their intake is allowed for, the difference is +6%.
By kind, against England (in brackets, once intake is allowed for): illness is 14% higher (2% higher), unauthorised absence 8% lower (8% higher), and severe absence 18% higher (18% higher).
What pushes absence up most here, against England, is ethnicity and language (+6% overall). What holds it down most is poverty (-8%). For illness, the biggest push is poverty (+8%).
West Sussex’s own effect, after intake: illness +4% (57th of 152 authorities), unauthorised +5% (52nd).









Figure 13: Why absence in West Sussex’s schools differs from England’s, group by group, autumn and spring 2025/26. Each group’s part is its national coefficients times the gap between the area’s and England’s average characteristics. Blue is what is left, the region, authority and the schools themselves. The parts add up on the log scale, so they are close to, but not exactly, additive as percentages.

For heads and governors
The national page sets out what the school’s part in absence is. In short:

Who runs a school, its size and its religious character make little difference to absence once intake is allowed for.
Schools with the same intake can differ a great deal, and the differences persist from year to year.

The table compares each of West Sussex’s schools with similar schools in its own authority, in 2024/25 and 2025/26. Click a school to open it in Find a twin, which finds its look-alikes across England, and the look-alikes that do much better.

9 schools have unauthorised absence more than 20% above similar schools in both years. That is the pattern worth asking about.
5 schools have unauthorised absence more than 20% below similar schools in both years. What they do may be worth sharing.

What goes with absence here
The national absence analysis models seven kinds of absence in every secondary school in England, using autumn and spring 2025/26 and the January 2026 census. Here it is applied to Rother’s 3 schools with full data. It compares them with England, with East Sussex and Sussex, and with the neighbouring districts (Hastings and Wealden).








Figure 12: Absence in Rother and its comparators against England’s average school, autumn and spring 2025/26. Hollow, the whole difference; filled, the part the schools’ intake, needs and setting do not account for (the national models’ region, authority and school effects). Schools in brackets.






Overall, Rother’s schools have 8% more absence than England’s average school. Once their intake is allowed for, the difference is -5%.
By kind, against England (in brackets, once intake is allowed for): illness is 7% higher (2% lower), unauthorised absence 26% higher (2% higher), and severe absence 37% higher (1% higher).
What pushes absence up most here, against England, is ethnicity and language (+11% overall). What holds it down most is the kinds of school (-1%). For illness, the biggest push is ethnicity and language (+7%).
East Sussex’s own effect, after intake: illness +10% (30th of 152 authorities), unauthorised +0% (83rd).

Each group’s part is its national coefficients times the gap between the area’s and England’s average characteristics. Blue is what is left, the region, authority and the schools themselves. The parts add up on the log scale, so they are close to, but not exactly, additive as percentages.

title: Independent schools
text:
ImportantIn short




There is no value added at 16 for independent schools, and one cannot fairly be built from published data. The two things that matter most in Value Added v2.1 are each school’s prior attainment and its disadvantage. Neither is published for independent schools, and nor is absence.
Their published GCSE results are not comparable either, but they can be completed. Many independent schools enter IGCSEs that do not count in the performance tables, so their Attainment 8 is often far below what their pupils achieve. A school’s average grade in the GCSEs that do count stands in well for the rest (Section 4). On it, the typical independent school sits between non-selective state schools and grammar schools.
One comparison does exist: value added at A level. DfE publishes 16-18 A level value added, from each student’s GCSE results, for 487 independent schools on the same basis as state sixth forms. It is the fair comparison available now, with caveats of its own.

title: Independent schools
text:
The sector
England has 1,606 open independent schools. This page is about the 898 mainstream independent schools that teach secondary ages, with about 396,000 pupils of all ages between them. The 2024/25 performance tables list 901 independent schools with pupils at the end of key stage 4 (a few have since closed or changed): 53,824 pupils, against 604,761 in state-funded mainstream schools, about 8% of the cohort. Independent special schools are a different sector and are left out.

Inspection: 652 are inspected by the Independent Schools Inspectorate (members of the associations) and 246 by Ofsted.
Admissions: 213 say they are selective, 229 non-selective, and 380 give no policy.
Single-sex: 160 girls’ schools and 91 boys’ schools.
Boarding: 286 have boarders.









Figure 1: Mainstream independent schools teaching secondary ages (GIAS, June 2026), coloured by A level value added 2024/25 (DfE, grades per entry; green above zero, purple below, as the explorer; grey, none published). Circle size by number of pupils.

Value Added v2.1 sets each school’s results against what its intake and setting would predict. This is what exists for independent schools, term by term:

The January 2026 school census publishes headcounts by age and sex, and boarders, for every independent school. It publishes none of the measures of who the pupils are: free school meals, first language, ethnicity and young carers are all blank. The only measures of need are SEN support and EHC plans. Independent schools identify more SEN support than state schools, mostly specific learning difficulties, and have far fewer EHC plans.

title: Independent schools
text:
The Attainment 8 problem








Figure 2: Attainment 8 per pupil, 2024/25 (performance tables, provisional): state-funded mainstream schools and independent mainstream schools with a published figure.





Independent schools, nearly all fee-paying and many selective, would be expected to have results well above the state average. Their published Attainment 8 has a median of 34.5, below the state median of 45.6, and 27% of independent schools score under 20. That does not reflect what their pupils achieve. Since 2017 the performance tables count only approved qualifications, and many independent schools enter their pupils for international GCSEs (IGCSEs), which are not on the list. A pupil with a string of top IGCSE grades can score next to nothing.
The same schools’ A level results show it:








Figure 3: Attainment 8 (2024/25) against A level average point score per entry (2024/25), schools with at least ten A level students. Dashed lines: the state-school bottom quarter on Attainment 8 and median on A levels.





In state schools, a school’s Attainment 8 and its A level results go together (correlation 0.76). In independent schools they are unrelated (0.03). 269 of the 461 independent schools with both (58%) are in the bottom quarter of state schools on Attainment 8 and above the state median at A level. Published Attainment 8 cannot be used to compare an independent school with anyone as it stands.

title: Independent schools
text:
Completing Attainment 8
The performance tables do not publish IGCSE results, so no published data put IGCSE grades and Attainment 8 side by side. But they do publish Attainment 8 in its parts, and that is enough to fill in what is missing.
Attainment 8 is English (counted twice), maths (counted twice), three EBacc slots (sciences, languages, humanities) and three open slots. The tables publish each school’s points in each, and how many of the EBacc and open slots its pupils fill on average. An IGCSE fills nothing. In independent schools:

English and maths: 33% score nothing for English and 43% nothing for maths. Every state school scores something for both.
The other six slots: pupils fill 4.4 on average, against 5.6 in state schools.

A school’s average grade per filled slot (the EBacc and open points divided by the slots filled) is measured the same way in both sectors. Unlike Attainment 8, it does not fall when slots are empty. It assumes a school’s pupils do about as well in their IGCSEs as in their GCSEs. To complete Attainment 8, English and maths are predicted from that grade, using the relationship in state schools, where they can always be counted:
\[\text{Attainment 8}_\text{completed} = 2\,\widehat{\text{English}} + 2\,\widehat{\text{maths}} + 6\,g\]
Does it work? Two tests:

In state schools, a school’s grade in its other subjects predicts its English grade with R² 0.88 and its maths grade with R² 0.90, to within about a third of a grade. The completed measure correlates with the real Attainment 8 at 0.98.
In independent schools, the average grade in counting GCSEs restores the link with the same schools’ A level results. It correlates with them at 0.84, against 0.03 for published Attainment 8, and 0.77 in state schools.









Figure 4: Average grade per counting GCSE slot, 2024/25: state non-selective schools, state grammar schools and independent schools. Schools where pupils fill less than half a slot on average are left out.













Figure 5: Independent schools: published Attainment 8 (left) and average grade in counting GCSEs (right) against the same schools’ A level points per entry, 2024/25, schools with at least ten A level students.

On the completed measure, the typical independent school’s pupils average about grade 6.3, against 4.7 in non-selective state schools and 7.3 in grammar schools: an Attainment 8 of about 62, between the two. That is attainment, not value added. It says nothing about what the schools add, because the intake terms are still missing (Section 5). Three cautions:

It assumes IGCSE grades match GCSE grades. If a school’s pupils do better or worse in their IGCSEs than in its GCSEs, the completed figure is off by that much. The A level check above suggests it is close on average, not for every school.
Pupils with nothing counted are invisible. A pupil who sat only IGCSEs adds no grade to the average. 7% of independent schools fill too few slots to compute it at all.
It is one year, provisional. The method can be repeated on each year’s tables.

section: Could a reduced model stand in?
text:
Could a reduced model stand in?
If the missing terms cannot be had, one could fit a model on only what independent schools do report (their neighbourhood, SEN, size, sex, selection, sixth form, region and setting) and compare results with that. We can test this where the answer is known: on state schools, against the full v2.1 model.

title: Independent schools
section: The comparison that exists: A level value added
text:
The comparison that exists: A level value added
DfE publishes value added at 16-18 for every school and college with A level students, independent schools included. It sets each student’s A level grades against those of students nationally with the same GCSE results, and averages by school, in grades per A level entry. Because it starts from each student’s own prior results, it allows for the largest thing the KS4 comparison cannot.

On this measure the typical independent school adds +0.17 of a grade per A level entry, against -0.05 in state school sixth forms. 49% of independent schools are clearly above zero, against 21% of state sixth forms. The spread within each sector is wider than the gap between them: many state sixth forms do better than the typical independent school.
What it does and does not allow for:

Prior attainment, yes, but GCSEs only. DfE’s technical guidance is explicit. For A levels, “students’ prior attainment is based on their average attainment in GCSEs only”, and only qualifications “approved for reporting in key stage 4 performance measures” count. So IGCSEs are left out of the baseline. A student with a mix is measured on their GCSEs alone. A student with only IGCSEs has no prior attainment and is left out of the value added, since a student “must have results at the end of key stage 4”. If many independent pupils were left out this way, independent schools would have fewer value-added entries per A level student than state schools. They have slightly more (2.70 against 2.58), so most of their students are in. For the many who mix, the baseline rests on their GCSE subjects only.
Disadvantage, no. DfE’s 16-18 value added has no adjustment for disadvantage or context. At GCSE the v2.1 model finds disadvantage worth a good deal even after prior attainment, so some of the independent schools’ lead is likely to be their intake rather than their teaching.
Who stays on, no. Sixth forms choose their students and students choose sixth forms. The two sectors’ A level cohorts are selected differently.
One year is noisy. Three-year averages are published alongside, and are steadier.

title: Independent schools
text:
Is a comparison possible?








Comparison
Possible?
Why




Value added at 16 on the v2.1 basis
No
No prior attainment, disadvantage or absence for independent schools, and an incomplete outcome


Published GCSE results (Attainment 8)
No
IGCSEs and other unapproved qualifications score nothing, so published figures are far too low for many schools


Completed Attainment 8 (average grade in counting GCSEs)
Yes, as attainment
Measured the same way in both sectors, validated against state schools and against independent schools’ own A level results; assumes IGCSE grades match GCSE grades; attainment, not value added


A reduced contextual model at 16
Not credibly
It can be computed, but in the state sector it gets value added badly wrong and credits advantaged intakes; independent intakes are the most advantaged of all


A level value added (16-18)
Yes, with caveats
Published by DfE for 487 independent schools on the same basis as state sixth forms; allows for prior attainment, not disadvantage or selection into the sixth form


A level results, raw
Descriptive only
Comparable qualifications, but no allowance for intake




What would make a fair comparison at 16 possible
All of these are about what is published, not about any individual pupil’s records:

Count what independent pupils sit. Publish Attainment 8 with IGCSEs and other GCSE-equivalent certificates included, beside the official figure, so the outcome is complete.
A starting point. A prior-attainment measure for independent schools’ pupils at entry, whether KS2 or an agreed baseline.
Who the pupils are. Some measure of disadvantage: bursary and fee-remission rates are the nearest equivalent to free school meals. First language, at least, as for state schools.
Attendance. Absence is the largest school-level term in v2.1, and independent schools are outside the collection.

Until then, the honest comparison is at A level, and it is a comparison of what sixth forms add to students who arrive with the same GCSEs, not of schools.

title: Find a twin
text:
NoteHow to use it




Choose a school. Pick a region, local authority or district, then a school within it.
Choose what to match on. Matching uses intake and setting only, never results or attendance. By default it weights what matters most for the measure you choose.
Closest twins are the schools most like yours anywhere in England.
Anti-twins are the look-alikes, from the 50 (or 25, or 100) most similar, that do furthest better than yours on the measure you choose:

lower absence of a kind;
higher value added or Attainment 8;
or absence and value added together.


Click a twin, in the chart, on the map or in the table, to compare its fact card with your school’s, including value added and absence year by year. Print for governors gives a clean copy of the comparison for a meeting. The address bar keeps your choice, so a link takes someone else to the same comparison.

title: Find a twin
text:
How the matching works
Every school is described by the characteristics the absence models use, in groups you can switch on or off:

Pupils: disadvantage (FSM), KS2 prior attainment, EAL, White British, joining mid-phase, and the share of girls.
Needs: SEN support, EHC plans, and social, emotional and mental health need.
Neighbourhood and place: neighbourhood education, and rural or urban.
The school: size, admissions, sixth form, and religious character.

For each measured characteristic, the difference between two schools is taken in standard deviations, capped at three. For each category, it is 0 if they match and 1 if not. The average across the characteristics is the distance, and similarity is one minus it, as a percentage. This is a form of Gower’s distance, as in the original project’s twin finder.
Weighting. By default each characteristic is weighted by how much it matters for the measure you chose. A school that matches yours on what drives that measure counts as more alike than one that matches on what does not. The weight is how much the characteristic moves the measure across schools: the standard deviation of its part in a regression of the measure on all the characteristics (log absence for absence). The weights are scaled to average one. Value added and Attainment 8 both take the Attainment 8 weights. Value added is already what is left once intake is allowed for, so the twins should match on what drives results. The combined measure takes the average of the overall absence and Attainment 8 weights. You can switch to equal weights.

title: What goes with school absence
text:
NoteWork in progress



This is the first cut of the absence analysis on the roadmap. It describes how absence varies between schools, and with what. It does not yet say why. Every figure comes from published school-level data, so every result is an association between schools, not an effect on pupils.

title: What goes with school absence
section: Why this matters for value added
text:
Why this matters for value added
Absence is the largest single term in Value Added v2.1’s expectation. The model takes each school’s absence as given: a school with more absence is expected to get lower results. That is fair to schools whose absence is outside their control. It is unfair if some of that absence is something the school could have prevented. To tell the two apart, we need to know what absence goes with. This page makes a start.

title: What goes with school absence
text:
What the research says
A research map of UK work since 2016 (summarised below; sources at the foot of the page) says absence is not one behaviour with one cause. Health, family, peer, school and wider circumstances all bear on it, and they interact. It is higher in secondary schools, rises with age, and is concentrated among pupils facing poverty, special educational needs, health difficulties and other disadvantage. Absence harms attainment whether or not it is authorised, but it is also a marker of difficulties that were already there.
The post-pandemic rise is real and not fully explained. The leading accounts are:

more illness;
anxiety and avoiding school;
broken routines and weaker attendance norms;
unmet SEND needs;
strained relations between home and school;
slow access to support.

No single cause has been shown to dominate.
Each strand of that research suggests something we can measure for every school in England:

title: What goes with school absence
section: How absence has changed, by reason
text:
How absence has changed, by reason








Figure 1: Absence by reason in England’s state-funded secondary schools, % of possible sessions, full years, 2016/17 to 2024/25 (sessions-weighted; DfE school-level absence data). 2019/20 was not collected; 2020/21 was a year of partial closure.













Figure 2: Persistent absence (missing 10% or more of sessions) and severe absence (50% or more), % of pupils, same schools and years.





The reasons have not moved together:

Illness jumped from 2.8% of sessions in 2018/19 to 5.2% in 2021/22. By 2024/25 it had fallen back to 3.7%, most of the way home.
Unauthorised absence other than holidays doubled, from 1.3% to 2.9% in 2023/24. It has barely come down since.
Severe absence rose every year, from 1.2% of pupils to 3.6%, nearly three times as many.

Persistent absence is falling, but the tail is still growing. That matches the research: the average can improve while the worst cases get worse.

title: What goes with school absence
text:
What absence is made of
Every missed session carries a register code, and DfE publishes them for each school. In the autumn and spring terms of 2025/26, illness and unauthorised absence together were most of it.

Suspension is a small part of it. Code E, a pupil suspended with no alternative provision, is 3.1% of absence, or 0.25 points. This is counted from the register, not estimated.
Schools that suspend more do have more absence of other kinds, but most of that is who their pupils are. Each extra suspension per 100 pupils goes with 0.043 points more non-suspension absence between schools, and 0.012 points when a school is compared with itself across years. It adds little to value added either. Absence adds 0.11 to the R² of Attainment 8 on top of suspension; suspension adds 0.005 on top of absence. So the model has no need of a suspension term. The full analysis is in Exclusions and Attendance.

title: What goes with school absence
section: What goes with absence, school by school
text:
What goes with absence, school by school
The model covers 3,147 state-funded secondary schools with full data. It uses their absence in the autumn and spring terms of 2025/26 and their intake as recorded in the January 2026 school census and SEN data. For each of seven outcomes, it is a multilevel model of the outcome (logged) on all the characteristics at once, with region and local authority effects.
Each number below is the difference in that kind of absence that goes with one standard deviation more of a characteristic, all else equal. A standard deviation is roughly the gap between a typical school and one noticeably above it. For yes-or-no characteristics, the number compares the two kinds of school. Purple means more absence, green less. Blank cells are differences that could be zero.








Figure 3: Difference in each kind of absence (%) with one standard deviation more of each characteristic (yes vs no for the categories), all else equal: multilevel models with region and local authority effects, 2025/26 autumn and spring terms. Purple, more absence; green, less. Blank, the 95% interval includes zero.





What stands out:

Poverty, prior attainment and mobility go with the absence a school has least claim to. With one SD more pupils on free school meals, unauthorised absence is +37% and severe absence +22%. Illness, once everything else is allowed for, is -9%. Lower KS2 prior attainment and more pupils joining mid-phase point the same way.
Among the types of need, social, emotional and mental health need is the one that matters. One SD more of it goes with +10% severe and +8% other authorised absence. Once the types of need are in the model, the share of pupils on SEN support or with EHC plans adds nothing more. This fits the research’s emphasis on anxiety and distress.
Schools with more White British pupils have more absence of every kind, especially severe (+30% per SD) and unauthorised (+12%). EAL goes the other way. This is a comparison between schools, not pupils. It matches the national statistics, where absence is lower among most minority ethnic groups. It does not say why.
Girls. Schools with more girls have more medical-appointment (+3%) and severe absence (+6%). This matches the research finding that girls are absent more than boys.
The school.

Selective schools have far less unauthorised (-37%) and severe absence (-48%) than intake alone predicts.
Schools with a religious character have somewhat less (-11% unauthorised).
Schools with a sixth form have more absence among their 11-16 pupils (+5% overall). This echoes Value Added v2.1, where 11-16 schools do better.
Being in a multi-academy trust makes little difference.

Place. Rural schools record +12% absence for medical appointments and -8% unauthorised absence, against urban schools near a city. A plausible reading is that getting to an appointment from a rural school costs a whole session rather than part of one. That bears on the distance-to-school question.
Young carers barely register. This is more likely a measurement problem than a finding: schools differ widely in how many young carers they identify.

title: What goes with school absence
text:
How much each group explains








Figure 4: Share of the variation between schools in each kind of absence (logged) explained by each group of characteristics: Shapley values of R² from OLS, region in Place. Each column sums to the total R² shown at the foot.





The kinds of absence split cleanly in two:

Unauthorised, persistent and severe absence are mostly about who the pupils are. Intake and school characteristics account for between 62% and 68% of the variation. Poverty, prior attainment and the school itself carry most of it.
Illness and medical appointments are mostly not. Only 30% and 24% is accounted for, and Place is the largest single group for both. Two schools with the same intake can record very different amounts of illness.

That is the case for v2.1’s sensitivity test that counts illness separately from other absence (Methodology).

title: What goes with school absence
text:
The school’s part
“The school” carries 13 to 14 points of R² for unauthorised, persistent and severe absence above. That does not mean schools are to blame for that much absence. The group is five measured features:

size;
whether the school has a sixth form;
its admissions (selective, or non-selective);
who runs it;
whether it has a religious character.

What schools do is not measured at all. Splitting the group into its five features shows where the credit goes:








Figure 5: The school group’s share of R², split into its five features: Shapley values with each feature as a player of its own and the other seven groups as before (OLS, region in Place), 2025/26 autumn and spring.





Most of it is selection. Admissions accounts for 9.2 of the points for unauthorised absence, 10.9 for persistent and 10.8 for severe. Selective schools choose their pupils. Prior attainment and free school meals measure some of what selection does, but not all of it, and admissions picks up the rest. That is a fact about who comes to the school, not about how it is run. Who runs it (2.6 points), size, sixth form and religious character each add little.
What a school does shows up somewhere else: in how far apart similar schools are. Take schools with the same intake, needs and setting, in the same local authority. What is left over (the models’ school-level residuals) is what the measured characteristics cannot explain. That includes how a school runs attendance, and also anything about its pupils the data does not see.




Table 2: How far apart schools with the same intake, needs and setting, in the same local authority, are on each kind of absence (2025/26 autumn and spring), and whether the differences repeat (the same models on 2024/25 full-year absence).

The gaps are large. Among otherwise similar schools in the same authority, the one a quarter of the way from the top has 53% more unauthorised absence than the one a quarter of the way from the bottom. For severe absence the gap is 67%; for overall absence, 24%.
They repeat. A school’s unexplained absence in 2025/26 correlates 0.81 with its own in 2024/25 for unauthorised absence, and 0.84 overall. Of the schools in the top quarter for unexplained unauthorised absence in 2025/26, 70% were in the top quarter the year before; chance would give 25%. These are stable features of schools or their communities, not noise.
That stability is not proof of a school effect. The same 2026 characteristics are used for both years, and pupils the data does not see are as stable as a school’s practice. Only following schools whose practice changed would separate the two.







TipFor heads and governors




Judge absence against what your intake predicts, not against the national average. The area pages give each Sussex school’s absence by kind, its prediction, and how it compares with similar schools in the same authority over two years.
Structure is not the lever. Being in a multi-academy trust, its size, and its religious character make little difference once intake is allowed for. Most of what looks like a “school” effect in the averages is selective admissions, which is about who is admitted.
Practice may well be the lever. Schools with the same intake differ by half again or more in unauthorised and severe absence, and the differences persist. A school well above similar schools, year after year, should ask what its look-alikes below the line are doing differently.
Look at the kind of absence. Unauthorised, persistent and severe absence are where similar schools differ most. Illness differs mostly by place, and partly by how readily it is authorised. Comparing schools on unauthorised absence alone falls hardest on those with poorer pupils.
The research points to where to look. It is consistent on:

early identification;
relationships and belonging;
support for social, emotional and mental health needs (the type of need that goes most with absence here);
work with families. Parental engagement is the one approach with consistent support from randomised trials, though most were in the United States.

Find a twin finds the schools in England most like yours in intake and setting. It also finds anti-twins: the look-alikes with much lower absence, or much higher value added. These are the schools worth calling.
Schools with a sixth form have +5% more absence among their 11-16 pupils than comparable 11-16 schools. That is worth a look in 11-18 schools.

title: What goes with school absence
section: Place, once the intake is allowed for

For most kinds of absence, a school’s region and authority matter little once its intake is known. Illness and other authorised absence are the exceptions: about 14% and 12% of the variation between schools is still at the region and authority levels after allowing for intake. Both are kinds of absence a school chooses to authorise. Some places’ schools record more illness than their intakes predict. That could be because their pupils really are ill more often. It could also be because schools in those places authorise absence as illness more readily, so that the same absence elsewhere would be recorded as unauthorised. The data cannot tell these apart.








Figure 6: Each local authority’s illness absence against what its schools’ intakes predict, 2025/26 autumn and spring (multilevel model, region and authority effects together). 152 authorities, lowest on the left; Sussex’s three are named.





Brighton and Hove records +27% more illness absence than its schools’ intakes predict, the 2nd highest of 152 authorities. Its unauthorised absence is -5% against intake (110th). The city’s high absence, which the Geographical effects page finds costs its pupils so little attainment, is illness absence, and its intake does not explain it. That leaves two readings: an unusual amount of illness, or a habit of authorising absence as illness that elsewhere would go unauthorised. Which it is matters for value added. If it is recording, the city’s absence is not the kind that costs attainment, and the model’s absence term over-forgives it. The next two sections take that further.

Illness or recording?
Authorities differ in how the same absence gets recorded, and the pattern follows disadvantage.

More disadvantaged authorities record less illness and more unauthorised absence. Total absence barely moves. Across authorities, illness and unauthorised absence correlate -0.46.
There is some real trade-off within authorities too. Following each authority over time, after allowing for national trends, one point more illness goes with 0.28 points less unauthorised absence (p = 0.024). If absence were simply being re-labelled, the figure would be close to one. It suggests that recording explains part of the difference between places, not all of it.

The same holds between pupils. In 2024/25, full year, illness was 32% of disadvantaged pupils’ absence in England and 52% of non-disadvantaged pupils’. Disadvantaged pupils still have more illness-coded absence, but their unauthorised absence is about four times as high.
Judging a school on unauthorised absence therefore falls hardest on schools with poorer pupils, whether or not those pupils miss more school.

It is the whole city. All ten schools are above England’s 3.67 on illness; the lowest is at 4.59.
The gap grew after the pandemic. It was 0.50 points in 2018/19 and is 1.74 now.
It is high for pupils of every kind. Disadvantaged pupils’ illness absence was 6.55% in 2024/25, full year, against 4.22% in England. For non-disadvantaged pupils it was 4.65% against 3.34%, and for all pupils 5.18% against 3.61%. Those rank 3rd, 2nd and 2nd of 150.
Re-labelling cannot be the whole story. Unauthorised absence is mid-table (65th of 150) and only slightly below what the city’s intake predicts, while illness is far above it. If schools here were turning truancy into illness, unauthorised absence would be low. For disadvantaged pupils it is high: 6.85% against 5.35%.

Code I means the school accepted the explanation given. It covers a chronic condition, a heavy cold, anxiety that makes the school gate impossible, and a parent saying “not well today”. The published data cannot separate them. The research’s emphasis on anxiety and the shape of the city’s pattern both point towards emotionally based school avoidance, but that is a hypothesis. Only the council’s and schools’ own records could test it.

title: What goes with school absence
text:
Is it a coastal problem?
The authorities with the largest illness excess look coastal: the Isle of Wight, South Tyneside, Brighton and Hove, Torbay. Census data from The Engagement Platform also reports weaker belonging and enjoyment among coastal secondary pupils, and a steeper fall in engagement between Year 7 and Year 8. That comes from a commercial provider, gives no sample sizes and has no attendance data, but belonging is exactly what this page cannot measure.
A school counts as coastal here if it is within 10 km of the sea, and an authority if at least half its sessions are in such schools. That makes 20 of 150 authorities coastal.

Illness is the one kind of absence clearly left. With everything on this page in the model, coastal schools have +4.7% illness absence (+0.8% to +8.7%), and persistent absence is +3.4%. Overall and unauthorised absence are indistinguishable from other schools. That is real, but small: about a sixth of a point of illness.
The wider gap is mostly who and where. Comparing whole authorities on disadvantage alone, coastal ones have 1.04 points more absence of all kinds. The table is stricter. Its models compare schools within regions and authorities, so a difference between whole authorities counts for less. That may go too far, and so may allowing for language, because few pupils with English as an additional language is partly what a coastal intake is. Taking language out, in the middle column, raises every figure a little.
It differs by pupil group. In 2024/25, allowing for each authority’s disadvantage, the coastal gap in all absence is 1.89 points for disadvantaged pupils, 0.50 for non-disadvantaged pupils and 1.04 for all pupils. For disadvantaged pupils most of it is unauthorised (1.06 points).
It does not explain Brighton and Hove. Adding a coastal term only takes the city’s excess from 1.72 points to 1.33, still 5th highest. Coastal authorities also vary hugely: illness is 5.70% on the Isle of Wight and 2.31% in Blackpool. Camden, with no coast, is among the highest.

The Year 7 to 8 pattern shows up in unauthorised absence, not illness. DfE publishes absence by year group for each authority, so the same pupils can be followed for a year, in the two cohorts up to 2024/25.

title: What goes with school absence
text:
The full models
Each of the seven outcomes has the same multilevel model. For school \(i\) in local authority \(j\) in region \(k\):
\[\log(y_{ijk} + 0.1) = \beta_0 + \sum_p \beta_p\, x_{p,ijk} + u_k + v_{jk} + e_{ijk}\]
\[u_k \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{region}}), \quad v_{jk} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{LA}}), \quad e_{ijk} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{school}})\]

The outcome \(y\) is a percentage: of possible sessions for the five kinds of absence, of pupils for persistent and severe. The 0.1 lets severe absence be zero.
The measured characteristics \(x\) are standardised to mean 0 and SD 1, so each \(\beta\) is the change in log absence for one SD, and \(100\,(e^{\beta} - 1)\) is the % difference shown in Figure 3.
The categories are compared with a reference: 11-16, non-selective in a selective area, maintained, no religious character, and urban near a major town or city.
Estimation is REML in lme4. The log-likelihoods, AIC and BIC are from the same models refitted by maximum likelihood. The marginal R² is the variance of the fixed-effect predictions over the total; the conditional R² adds the region and authority effects (Nakagawa and Schielzeth). “Explained by the characteristics” is the fall in total variance from the model with no characteristics.

title: What goes with school absence
text:
What this cannot tell us

Schools, not pupils. A school with more pupils on free school meals having more absence does not show that its pupils on free school meals are the ones absent.
Association, not cause. Some of the school characteristics may follow from absence rather than lead to it, such as a school’s size or who runs it.
Two terms of one year. Autumn and spring carry more illness than summer, and one year is a snapshot. The trend figures are full years.
Measured needs only. SEN data counts identified need. The research warns that unmet or unidentified need sits outside it, and so do young carers not known to their school.
School climate is unmeasured. Belonging, bullying, relationships and fit come out of the research as important, and nothing here measures them.
Reasons are published by place, not by pupil group within a school. The disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged figures are for whole authorities, for full years up to 2024/25, so they do not line up exactly with the 2025/26 school figures.
Coastal is a judgement. The 10 km line treats estuaries narrower than 10 km as land, which leaves Southampton inland. Large counties such as Devon have many coastal schools but fall below the half-way mark.

title: What goes with school absence
text:
Next steps

Within-school change. Started: How school absence changes follows every school from 2016/17 to 2025/26, tests whether absence moves when intake does, and looks at academy conversion and changes of trust.
Illness or recording? Started: Illness or recording? finds a partial trade-off. Separating the two for good needs records that say what lies behind code I, such as anxiety against infection, and whether a few pupils or many are behind it.
Distance to school, from the roadmap. The rural appointments result gives a first reason to expect it to matter.
The severe tail. Severe absence is rising while the average falls. It needs its own model.
Back into value added. Absence against intake, split by kind, could replace raw absence in a future version of the model.

title: What goes with school absence
text:

The research summary draws on a research map of UK work since 2016 (compiled with Elicit), including:

title: Distance to school
text:
ImportantIn short




Across England, children in deprived neighbourhoods usually live closer to a secondary school. That holds in cities, towns and the countryside, and in 81% of districts.
Brighton and Hove is the other way round. Children in the most deprived third of its neighbourhoods live 1.57 km from their nearest school, in a straight line, and the rest live 1.18 km. That is 33% further, the 5th largest difference of 293 districts proportionately and the 2nd largest in kilometres. Among the 109 mostly urban local authorities, none has its deprived neighbourhoods further from a school.
Absence goes with distance, more for disadvantaged pupils, in every year tested. Across 150 authorities and six years from 2018/19, disadvantaged pupils’ absence is 3.5 points higher for each extra kilometre between deprived neighbourhoods and a school, against 0.6 for non-disadvantaged pupils and 1.7 for all pupils. It holds on eleven measures of distance and is far weaker in primary schools, as it should be if the journey to secondary school matters.
But most of that slope is who lives in those places, not the journey. Given the ethnic mix of disadvantaged pupils in each authority, the slope falls to 0.6, and with every control to 0.3, with an interval that includes zero. Ethnic mix is a confounder here: places with schools close together tend to have disadvantaged pupils from groups who attend more.
A smaller link remains in three separate tests. In mostly urban authorities outside London, the slope for disadvantaged pupils is still 2.5 points per kilometre given ethnic mix and region, against 0.4 in primary schools. Within one authority, pupils in the most deprived neighbourhoods have 0.45 points more absence per kilometre. And each doubling of how far a school’s nearest children live goes with 0.26 points more absence in every year, given the school’s intake and ethnic make-up, and more where more pupils are on free school meals. For disadvantaged pupils the link is mainly with unauthorised and persistent absence, not illness. These are associations, not proof of cause.
Moving a school would change this. A school back on CoMArt’s old site, or Longhill moved to the top of Elm Grove, would bring the deprived neighbourhoods of Brighton and Hove to about 1.19 to 1.21 km and close most of the gap.
Real journeys tell the same story for Brighton and Hove. By walking and bus, children in its most deprived neighbourhoods are 4.7 minutes further from a school than the rest, and walking alone 9.0 minutes. No comparator place is more than 1.3 minutes further by walking and bus, and its deprived neighbourhoods need the most changes of bus. See journey times.
Among all 109 mostly urban authorities, none has its deprived neighbourhoods as far from a school by walking and bus. The next largest gaps are Tameside (3.7 minutes) and Derby (3.4 minutes), and in the median authority the deprived third is nearer. It is mostly distance, not slow buses, but 18% of those journeys need two or more buses, the most of any authority. See the 109 authorities.
Across those authorities, distance still goes with disadvantaged absence, and the rest of the journey adds little. With every control, 1.9 points per kilometre (2.5 outside London), and little in primary. Journey time does not beat straight-line distance, and changes of bus, waiting and missing a bus add nothing once distance is known. The climb on the walk home, and busy change points (mostly in London), are hints that need more testing. School buses show no general link either: Longhill, where missing the last workable journey means arriving about 17 minutes late, is a striking case, not a pattern.
What it could mean for GCSE results. If the extra absence is caused by the journey, each kilometre would cost disadvantaged pupils about 2.2 to 2.7 Attainment 8 points, and Brighton and Hove’s gap about 1. That is about the lower end of Gorard and Siddiqui’s estimate of what mixing intakes could gain, 1 to 3 points. GCSE results do not show the distance cost directly. See GCSE results.
The admissions changes themselves did little either way. On the city’s school system model, the 2024 map and priority 6 together lengthened disadvantaged children’s journeys by about 0.4 minutes and lowered segregation by about 6%. In Attainment 8 points that is a journey cost of about 0.06 against a generous mixing gain of up to 0.20: both a fraction of a point. The gap comes from where the schools are. The council’s first proposal, priority 6 at 20% with Dorothy Stringer and Blatchington Mill cut to 300, would have lengthened journeys a little more and displaced more children, for no gain in mixing, and 30% would have done no more than 20%. See the admissions changes and the proposals.
Most of this page is in straight lines. They ignore hills, bus routes and catchments, and a child’s nearest school need not be the one they attend. Every source and calculation is in the methodology.

title: Distance to school
text:
What this measures
How far each school’s own pupils travel is not published, so this page starts from where children live and where schools are. This is a summary: the methodology gives every source, vintage and formula.

Schools. Every open state-funded secondary, all-through and middle deemed secondary school in England in the DfE’s register, Get Information About Schools (June 2026): 3,282 schools taking pupils at 13 or younger and keeping them to at least 16. Special schools, pupil referral units and independent schools are left out.
Neighbourhoods. England’s 33,755 Census 2021 Lower Layer Super Output Areas, each placed at the mean of its Output Areas’ population-weighted centroids. Averages are weighted by the 10 to 14 year olds living there.
Deprivation. The share of households deprived in two or more of the Census’s four dimensions (employment, education, health, housing), the same measure as the neighbourhood covariates.
Distance. The straight line to the nearest school. Each place’s neighbourhoods are split into its most deprived third and the rest, so the comparison is always within one place.
Kind of place. The ONS 2021 rural-urban classification. A district or authority is “mostly urban” if at least 80% of its 10 to 14 year olds live in urban neighbourhoods.

Schools in Wales are not in the register used here, so a few neighbourhoods on the border look further from a school than they are.

title: Distance to school
section: Across England, deprived neighbourhoods are nearer
text:
Across England, deprived neighbourhoods are nearer
Within each kind of place, the most deprived neighbourhoods tend to be among the closest to a school. One likely reason is that they are usually denser and more central.








Figure 1: Mean straight-line distance from home to the nearest state secondary school, by how deprived the neighbourhood is (England’s tenths, 10 = most deprived) and the ONS 2021 rural-urban class of the neighbourhood. Weighted by 10 to 14 year olds.





Taken across England as a whole, children in the most deprived third of neighbourhoods live 1.00 km from a school and the rest 1.75 km. Much of that is town against country, which is why the rest of this page compares neighbourhoods within one place.

title: Distance to school
text:
Does absence go with distance?
FFT Education Datalab compared pupils within schools, using straight-line distance from their home postcodes. Those living furthest away were absent slightly more often, and the difference was wider for disadvantaged pupils. FFT calls distance “a relatively minor factor” and suggests that travel times may be instructive. Published data allow several further tests. Every source and calculation is set out in the methodology.

A first look: by authority, for all three groups
DfE publishes absence by disadvantage for each local authority, so the distance from deprived neighbourhoods to a school can be set against absence for each group of pupils.

It is the distance that goes with absence, not the gap within the authority. Added to the same model, how much further the deprived neighbourhoods are than the rest has no clear relationship with absence for any group (disadvantaged t = -0.4, non-disadvantaged t = -1.4, all pupils t = -0.3). Fairness in access and the level of access are separate questions.
One year, one measure and three controls cannot carry much weight. The rest of this section tries to break the result.


How firm is it?

Given the ethnic mix of each group of pupils it falls by about four-fifths, and with every control no clear slope is left across all authorities. A smaller link remains in mostly urban authorities, within authorities for the most deprived neighbourhoods, and between schools.

The slope for disadvantaged pupils is positive in all six years, from 2.3 to 4.5 points per kilometre. It was already there before the pandemic (+2.3 in 2018/19) and has been larger since 2021/22. Distance is recalculated each year from school opening and closing dates, so earlier years are not measured against today’s schools. The network has grown from 3,226 schools in September 2018 to 3,289 in September 2025.

To avoid resting on any one choice, the same model was fitted on every combination of 6 years, 11 measures of distance, 6 sets of controls and 5 samples of authorities, for each group of pupils: 1,980 models per group, shown in Figure 7. Which neighbourhoods’ distance matters is also informative. Put the deprived neighbourhoods and the others in one model, and for disadvantaged pupils the deprived neighbourhoods’ distance carries about twice the weight (+3.1 against +1.6 per kilometre). For non-disadvantaged pupils the two are about equal (+0.4 and +0.4).
The relationship is not a straight line, either. Compared with authorities under 1 km, disadvantaged absence is 1.8 points higher at 1 to 1.5 km and 2.2 at 1.5 to 2 km, but only 0.7 at 2 to 3 km, where there are just 4 authorities, all large and rural.


What takes the slope away?
Controls overlap, so adding them one by one cannot say which one matters. Figure 8 splits the fall from the first model to the fullest into a part for each block of controls, using a method that does not depend on the order they go in (a Gelbach decomposition; details).








Figure 8: How much of the fall in the slope, from the model with share and urbanity to the model with every control, each block of controls accounts for, in points of absence per kilometre, all years pooled, with 95% bootstrap intervals. The parts add up to the whole fall. Below zero, a block would make the slope larger if taken away.





It is ethnic mix, and very little else. Of the fall from 3.52 to 0.34 points per kilometre for disadvantaged pupils, ethnic mix and language account for 3.01. Region adds 0.69, almost all of it London. Without London region adds nothing (-0.05), and ethnic mix accounts for all of the fall (1.72, against a fall of 1.63, since the other parts are slightly negative overall). Density, health, cars, deprivation and needs each do little once ethnic mix is held, and their parts roughly cancel.
Figure 9 shows it directly, using DfE’s count of pupils by ethnicity and free school meals in each authority, so that each group of pupils is compared on its own ethnic mix.








Figure 9: The slope of absence on distance, all years pooled, with 95% intervals, as controls are added. Ethnic mix is the shares of that group of pupils who are White British, Asian, Black and of mixed heritage, by authority and year. Points of absence per kilometre.





Why would ethnic mix do this? In 2024/25 the White British share of an authority’s disadvantaged pupils correlates with how far its deprived neighbourhoods are from a school (r = 0.69), since diverse places tend to be dense places with schools close together. On its own that share accounts for 63% of the variation in disadvantaged absence between authorities. So where schools are close, disadvantaged pupils also tend to be from groups with higher attendance, and a simple plot such as Figure 5 credits distance with that. This says nothing about why attendance differs between groups: ethnic mix stands in for migration histories, family and community ties and much else, none of which the data can separate.
Confounding or mediation? A mediator lies on the path: distance would change it, and it would change absence. A confounder drives both. The evidence points to confounding.

A longer journey to school does not change the ethnic mix of a place, so ethnic mix cannot sensibly be a mediator of distance. It is a confounder, or composition.
The obvious candidates for mediation contribute little. Households with no car and population density barely move the slope once ethnic mix is held (Figure 8). That does not rule out mediation, because authority-wide averages are a poor measure of how any one family travels.

The test of composition is whether the link holds within one ethnic group. DfE publishes absence by ethnic group for each authority, though not split by disadvantage.

A clear link among disadvantaged White British pupils could be hidden inside a flat line for all White British pupils. DfE publishes nothing that would show it.

Across all authorities, no clear slope is left for any group: +0.34 for disadvantaged pupils, with an interval from -0.6 to +1.2. Adding distance to that model leaves its fit unchanged (R² 0.881 to 0.881). But that interval does not mean zero. It still allows a little over one point per kilometre, and the controls account for 76% of the variation in distance, so the model has little left to work with, and 28 terms for 150 authorities.
The link survives further in towns and cities. In mostly urban authorities it is +1.92 with every control (t = 2.6). Outside London it is +2.53 given ethnic mix and region (t = 4.4), and +1.16 with every control, when its interval includes zero. In less urban authorities there is nothing at any stage.
Other designs are not subject to this limit, and they are in the sections that follow. Within authorities the link stays in the most deprived neighbourhoods given Census character, including their White British residents (below). At school level it survives the school’s own ethnic make-up in every year (below).


A falsification test: primary schools
If the link is about getting to a secondary school, the distance to a secondary school should say little about absence in primary schools. If it is about the place, it should predict both. The same children and families are involved, so this is a sharp test.








Figure 10: The distance from deprived neighbourhoods to a secondary school against absence in secondary schools, in primary schools, and the step up between them in the same authority and year, all years pooled, with 95% intervals. Points of absence per kilometre, allowing for the share disadvantaged and how urban the authority is.





It passes on these controls. For disadvantaged pupils the slope is +3.5 in secondary schools and +0.5 in primary, and it is +3.0 on the step up from primary to secondary within the same authority and year, which sets aside anything about a place that affects both phases. For non-disadvantaged pupils the primary slope is -0.3, below zero. The step up is steeper for disadvantaged pupils than for non-disadvantaged pupils by 2.2 points per kilometre (t = 5.3), or 0.7 without London (t = 2.0).
The small primary slope for disadvantaged pupils is not zero, which suggests some of the secondary slope is the place. Distance to a primary school itself goes with primary absence for disadvantaged pupils (+1.8 per kilometre, t = 2.1), though primary schools are so close that a kilometre is a long way. The test is less clear once ethnic mix is held, because the difference in attendance between ethnic groups is itself wider in secondary school than in primary. Across all authorities the step up for disadvantaged pupils falls to +0.42 (t = 1.0). In mostly urban authorities outside London the test still passes: given ethnic mix and region, +2.5 in secondary, +0.4 in primary, and +2.0 on the step up (t = 3.3).


Within the same authority
Everything so far compares one authority with another, so anything about a whole place can be mistaken for distance. A second DfE data set offers a stronger test. For 2023/24 and 2024/25 it gives absence by where pupils live, not where they go to school, in each authority, by the national tenth of the Income Deprivation Affecting Children Index (IDACI) of their home neighbourhood. Those tenths can be matched to the distance from the same neighbourhoods, giving 2,898 groups of pupils in 150 authorities. The number of pupils in each group lines up closely with the Census count of children (r = 0.99). DfE does not split this file by disadvantage, so it describes all pupils living in each kind of neighbourhood.
Brighton and Hove stands out in it (Figure 11). Across England, children in the most deprived neighbourhoods live nearest a school. In Brighton and Hove they live furthest away, and absence and persistent absence climb much more steeply with deprivation than in England.








Figure 11: Pupils in state-funded secondary schools, 2024/25, by the national IDACI tenth of the neighbourhood where they live (1 = most deprived): straight-line distance to a school, overall absence, and the share who are persistently absent. All pupils; DfE does not publish this by disadvantage. DfE, absence by pupil residence; IoD 2019; Census 2021; Get Information About Schools.





The children in the city’s most deprived tenth of neighbourhoods live 1.93 km from a school, against 1.01 km for that tenth across England. They miss 17.8% of sessions against 11.0%, and 49% are persistently absent against 32%.

Three things follow.

Most of the slope between authorities is not there within them. For the most deprived three tenths it is +2.5 per kilometre between authorities, and +0.21 within them, or +0.45 given Census character. Part of that fall will be noise, because the distance for a tenth of an authority’s neighbourhoods is a rough average of places that can be far apart. Even so, the safer reading is that most of the slope between authorities is about the authorities, which fits what ethnic mix does above. Holding Census character raises the slope, because within an authority the further neighbourhoods tend to be less urban and less dense (r = -0.51 and -0.46), and differ little in their White British share (r = 0.10). So the clearer estimate depends on that adjustment: without it the interval includes zero.
What remains is where it should be. Within authorities, given Census character, the link is clear only for pupils in the most deprived three tenths. It is steeper there than in the least deprived three tenths by 0.59 points per kilometre (t = 3.1). It is similar in each year (+0.48 and +0.41), without London (+0.48) and without Brighton and Hove (+0.41).
It is much weaker in primary schools. In the same neighbourhoods the primary slope is +0.14, with an interval that includes zero, against +0.45 in secondary. The persistent absence result is +1.6 points of pupils per kilometre in secondary (t = 3.7) and +0.5 in primary (t = 1.6).

Schools whose nearest children live further away have lower results than their intake predicts, by more for disadvantaged pupils (-1.1% for each doubling) than for non-disadvantaged pupils (-0.7%) or all pupils (-0.5%). Allowing for absence takes away about half of that for disadvantaged pupils. These are small differences, and part of what they measure may be the kind of place rather than the journey.


What it adds up to
Taking the tests together:

Firm: the pattern. Disadvantaged absence goes with distance in every year from 2018/19 and on every measure of distance, and it is much weaker in primary schools.
Firm: most of the slope in Figure 5 is not distance. Ethnic mix accounts for nearly all of the fall across authorities, and is a confounder rather than a step on the path from distance to absence.
Likely: a smaller link of its own. It appears in mostly urban authorities given ethnic mix and region, within authorities for pupils in the most deprived neighbourhoods, and between schools given their intake and ethnic make-up. It shows up in unauthorised and persistent absence. Three different designs, with different weaknesses, point the same way.
Not established: that distance causes it. Network changes point the right way, but the estimates are imprecise and those changes are not random.

Brighton and Hove’s disadvantaged pupils are close to the median authority for ethnic mix (64% White British, against 66%), so ethnic mix does not explain its high absence. Given mix, region, share and urbanity, the city is 2.5 points above expectation, 6th of 150 authorities, and given distance too it is 2.1 above, still 6th. So on this model distance explains only about 0.4 points of why the city stands out.
Its deprived neighbourhoods are 0.59 km further from a school than those of the median mostly urban authority outside London. On the urban estimates, from 1.2 with every control to 2.8 given ethnic mix, region and density, that would go with about 0.7 to 1.7 points of disadvantaged absence, out of the 4.8 by which the city is above England. On the within-authority estimate, for all pupils in deprived neighbourhoods, it would be about 0.2. So distance is a credible part of the city’s problem, and not the main explanation for it. Journey times on the real networks may show more, because Brighton’s hills and bus routes are what straight lines miss most.

title: Distance to school
section: What this cannot say, and what comes next
text:
What this cannot say, and what comes next

Straight lines are not journeys. Hills, the sea, bus routes and bus fares are all missing, and they may matter most in places like Brighton and Hove.
The nearest school is not the school attended. Catchments, admissions and choice decide that. FFT measured from pupils’ own postcodes; here distance describes where schools and children are.
These are comparisons between places and schools, so they show patterns, not what would happen to one child’s attendance if their journey changed. DfE publishes absence by disadvantage only down to authority level, and the file by home neighbourhood does not split by disadvantage.

Next on the roadmap:

The children whose journeys the admissions changes lengthened most, such as those in Whitehawk, rather than the city’s average, from the school system model.
Better school-level measures. A gravity model of who goes where would improve on “nearest children”, until a published measure of how far each school’s pupils travel exists.
Real bell times, and the climb and the busy change points tested again with them.
Rail, Metro and tram timetables for London and the large conurbations, where buses alone overstate journeys.

title: Neighbourhood types
text:
ImportantIn short




For results, the classification is another way of measuring the same thing. A school’s mix of neighbourhood types reproduces the neighbourhood education term almost exactly. Used instead of it, it explains results as well. Used as well as it, it adds next to nothing.
Within a local authority it explains nothing more about value added, at any of the three tiers. Schools that do better than similar schools in their own authority do not sit in different kinds of neighbourhood.
Between places there is something, and mostly for disadvantaged pupils. Disadvantaged pupils do better where schools sit among multicultural, urban neighbourhoods. They do worse among the classification’s “Baseline UK”, legacy industrial and coastal, and small-town neighbourhoods. This describes the kinds of place behind the local authority effects. It does not add a new term to the model. The classification’s groups explain 11.5% of disadvantaged pupils’ value added, against 2.3% for non-disadvantaged pupils and 2.8% for all pupils.
The multicultural lead belongs to disadvantaged pupils alone. Non-disadvantaged pupils get no such lead. The shortfall in small-town and coastal neighbourhoods looks shared, school by school, but it is weak between authorities.
The finest tier is not needed. Groups (21 classes) find what subgroups (52) find; supergroups (8) find less.

title: Neighbourhood types
text:
The classification and the neighbourhoods
The 2021/2 Output Area Classification sorts every Output Area in the UK into one of 8 supergroups, 21 groups and 52 subgroups. It clusters dozens of Census variables on population, households, housing, ethnicity, migration, education, work and health. Neighbourhood education in Value Added v2.1 is one Census variable: the share of adults with degree-level qualifications.
To compare like with like, each school’s neighbourhood here is the same as for neighbourhood education: the 150 Output Areas whose centres are nearest the school. A category has no median, so each school’s neighbourhood is described by its profile: the share of those 150 areas in each class, at each tier. It is also described by how mixed they are (the entropy of the subgroup shares). 3,262 schools have both value added and a profile.
