The other v2.1 terms explain 81.9% of the variation in results. Neighbourhood education takes that to 83.6%. The classification’s subgroups on their own reach 83.5%, about the same. Adding them to neighbourhood education gives 83.8%, a gain of under a quarter of a point. The reason is that the profile is, very largely, neighbourhood education: the subgroup shares predict a school’s neighbourhood education with R² 0.90 out of sample (groups 0.85, supergroups 0.65).

title: Neighbourhood types
text:
Does it explain value added?
Value added is what the v2.1 model cannot explain. If the classification picked up a neighbourhood effect the model misses, it would explain some of it. The test is in two forms:

Against England, which includes each school’s region and local authority effects.
Within the local authority, the school’s own part only.









Figure 1: Share of the variation in value added explained out of sample by region, by the classification’s profile at each tier, and by both (10-fold cross-validation, repeated). Value added is each school’s average over its years, v2.1.






Within the authority, nothing. At every tier, the classification explains about none of a school’s value added relative to its own authority, for all, disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils. Schools that do better than similar schools nearby do not sit in different kinds of neighbourhood.
Against England, something, because value added against England includes the place a school is in. For all pupils, region explains 4.8% and region with the subgroups 7.9%. Non-disadvantaged pupils are about the same, at 5.2% and 8.3%. For disadvantaged pupils the step is larger: 8.4% with region alone, and 15.1% with region and groups.

So the classification describes places, not schools within them. Local authorities, entered directly, explain 16.0% of disadvantaged pupils’ value added. The classification’s groups alone explain 11.5%, most of that. For all pupils, the authorities explain 10.8% and the groups only 2.8%. For non-disadvantaged pupils, they explain 10.6% and 2.3%.

title: Neighbourhood types
text:
What kinds of place








Figure 2: Correlation of each local authority’s effect in value added (v2.1) with the share of its schools’ neighbourhoods in each supergroup and in selected groups, weighted by the number of schools, for all, disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils.





For disadvantaged pupils, authorities do better the more their schools sit among multicultural neighbourhoods:

Challenged Multicultural Communities and Students (group 4c, +0.34);
Low-Skilled Migrant and Student Communities (supergroup 4, +0.29).

They do worse the more their schools sit among the classification’s Baseline UK neighbourhoods (supergroup 6, -0.28), Inner Suburbs and Small Town Living (2a, -0.23) and Legacy Industrial and Coastal Communities (6b, -0.20).
For non-disadvantaged pupils the same correlations are much weaker. None goes beyond 0.12 either way (4c +0.10, 6 -0.07, 6b -0.12). The pattern between authorities is a pattern for disadvantaged pupils.
This matches what is known about where disadvantaged pupils do well: in London and other diverse cities, much less so in coastal and former industrial towns. Neighbourhood education does not capture it, because the two kinds of place can have similar qualification levels. These are correlations with authority effects. They describe the places; they do not say what about them matters.








Figure 3: Value added (against England, %) of a school whose 150 nearest Output Areas were all of one group, for all, disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils: shares of each group with no intercept, with 95% intervals, ordered by disadvantaged pupils’ estimate. Pale: fewer than 50 schools have a fifth or more of their neighbourhood in the group, so the estimate leans on extrapolation.





School by school, the pure-type estimates mostly tell the same story for disadvantaged pupils. Multicultural groups (4c, 3b, 3c, 4b) sit above zero. Small-town, coastal, rural-amenity and challenged groups (2a, 2b, 6b, 1b, 6a) sit below. Two groups do not fit: Established but Challenged (7a) and Spacious Rural Living (1a) carry large positive estimates here, but show no relationship at all with authority effects. They are probably particular places rather than a pattern, and are best left aside until they can be looked at area by area.
Non-disadvantaged pupils share only one side of this. The multicultural lead is not theirs: Challenged Multicultural Communities (4c) is at +1.9% against +11.3% for disadvantaged pupils, and 3b at -5.4% against +9.9%. The small-town and coastal shortfall does appear: 6b at -8.7%, 1b at -8.2% and 2a at -6.9%. Because the correlations between authorities are weak for these pupils, treat that as a school-level estimate, with the limits below, not as a place effect.

title: Neighbourhood types
text:
Mixed neighbourhoods
Is it the mix rather than the type? Schools whose 150 Output Areas are more varied have slightly lower value added against England, region for region. One standard deviation more mixing goes with -0.7% Attainment 8. That is small, and is not pursued here.

Going down to subgroups adds little. The signal is in the broad kinds of place: diverse urban areas on one side, small-town, coastal and former industrial areas on the other. Those differ at the group level.

title: Neighbourhood types
text:
What it means for v2.1

No change to the expectation. The classification adds nothing to results beyond neighbourhood education, and nothing to value added within authorities. There is no case for putting it in the model.
It helps read the local authority effects. Part of why disadvantaged pupils do better in some authorities than others goes with the kind of neighbourhoods their schools serve. Far less of it does for non-disadvantaged pupils. That is a description of place, and it is where the Brighton and Hove effect and its causes belong.
For the next Census variables. The classification is mostly education and deprivation, which the model already has. The part it adds is ethnic diversity and the urban/coastal character of a place. Census variables on those, rather than more on qualifications, are the ones worth trying.

title: Neighbourhood types
text:
What this cannot tell us

A school’s neighbourhood is not its pupils’ homes. The 150 nearest Output Areas stand for the area a school serves; pupils at selective, faith and popular schools come from further away.
The classes are bundles. Each is a cluster of many variables, so a class effect cannot say which variable matters.
Pure-type estimates extrapolate. Few schools sit in one class alone; the shares model reads off what a school surrounded by one type would get.
One cross-section. Profiles are from the 2021 Census and value added is averaged over 2021/22 to 2024/25.

Built by R/11_oac_neighbourhoods.R from the 2021/2 Output Area Classification (Wyszomierski, Longley, Singleton, Gale and O’Brien, The Geographical Journal).

title: Geographical effects
text:
NoteIn short



On the v2.1 model Brighton and Hove has the 6th largest local authority effect of 152: its schools’ Attainment 8 runs +3.7% above what intake and context predict, after neighbourhood education is taken into account. Almost all of it is an absence effect. The city’s absence is among the highest in England, the model expects that absence to cost attainment, and in Brighton and Hove it costs much less than expected. Take absence out of the model and the authority falls to 59th. The extra absence is mostly authorised illness. Why it costs so little here is the open question, and family-level resources are one of the likely answers.



How large, and how steady
The effect is there for every group of pupils and in every year:

It is an absence effect
The test is to refit the model one term at a time. Each row below is the all-pupils model with one change, on the 12,763 school-years that have published absence reasons:

Without absence the effect falls from +3.7% to +0.6%, indistinguishable from zero.
Without neighbourhood education or without prior attainment it grows, to +5.5% and +6.9%. Both are already working: the city’s intakes are more advantaged on both, and the model credits that. See neighbourhood education below.
Local segregation changes nothing. Brighton and Hove’s catchment admissions, with random allocation as a tie-break, keep its schools relatively mixed, but that does not explain the effect.
The 11–16 flag, added in v2.1, takes a little off: without it, as in v2.0, the effect is +3.8%. 60% of Brighton and Hove’s school-years are at 11–16 schools, against 37% in England, and nationally 11–16 schools score +1.0% higher.

The arithmetic. Over 2021/22 to 2024/25, the four years the model is fitted on, Brighton and Hove’s schools average 10.9% full-year absence against 9.0% for England (means of school-years), 6th highest of 152 authorities. In 2024/25 alone, the year the area page’s add-and-take figure uses, it was 11.3% against 8.6% (means of schools): the gap has widened. On the v2.1 absence coefficient (-0.225, an elasticity), that difference lowers expected Attainment 8 by 4.5%. The authority effect, +3.7%, almost exactly gives it back. Brighton and Hove’s schools attain about what similar intakes attain elsewhere. They do it despite absence that, elsewhere, goes with lower results.
Inside the city, absence costs about what it costs elsewhere. A school with more absence than its neighbours does worse by about the national rate: the interaction is +0.034 (standard error 0.042). It is the city’s level of absence that carries no penalty, not its slope.


What kind of absence

Of Brighton and Hove’s 1.9 points of extra absence, 1.4 is authorised illness. Unauthorised absence is close to England’s. Illness makes up 57% of absence in the city (36th highest share of 152).
Nationally, illness absence costs less than other absence. Split in two, a 1% rise in illness absence goes with -0.06% Attainment 8 and a 1% rise in other absence with -0.12%. Allowing for that takes some of the effect away: to +3.5% with the illness share, +2.6% with absence split. It does not take most of it away. Absence’s type, as DfE records it, is part of the story, not the whole of it.


Neighbourhood education
v2.1 measures neighbourhood education as the share of adults with a degree-level (level 4+) qualification in the 150 Census output areas nearest each school, from the 2021 Census. It is there because a school’s results follow the education of the families around it, and FSM sees only the bottom of that.
Where the city’s schools sit. Their neighbourhoods average 43.4% of adults at level 4+, against 33.2% around England’s schools: about 1.0 standard deviation higher, 25th of 152 authorities. The share with no qualifications is 13.9% against 18.8%. 9 of the city’s 10 schools sit above England’s median school:

Each standard deviation of neighbourhood education is worth +2.44% of Attainment 8 for all pupils, +2.58% for non-disadvantaged pupils and only +0.82% for disadvantaged ones. Set against England, the city’s neighbourhoods lift its schools’ expected Attainment 8 by about +1.1 points for all pupils, +1.3 for non-disadvantaged and +0.3 for disadvantaged pupils. That is credit the schools do not get: it is in the expectation, not in their value added.
Without the term, the authority effect would be +5.5% (3rd) rather than +3.7%. Neighbourhood education already accounts for about 32% of what would otherwise look like a city effect.
Would a better measure take more? The table refits the model with the neighbourhood drawn at every scale the original project built, and with the share of adults with no qualifications:

No. A more local neighbourhood fits worse at every step, and leaves the city’s effect larger: +4.7% with the 5 nearest output areas. The no-qualifications share fits worse than level 4+. The best fit, level 4+ and no qualifications, 150 nearest, moves the effect only to +3.6%. Neighbourhood education is doing what it can, and the rest is not a neighbourhood the Census can see.
What it cannot see. The measure counts every adult, not parents. Brighton and Hove has two universities: students, whose highest qualification while studying is usually level 3, and young graduates without school-age children both sit in the count, in opposite directions, and neither says much about the families whose children attend the schools. A measure of parents’ qualifications, from the Census tables for households with dependent children, would test this directly (reading 1 below).


Would different admissions change it?
Because neighbourhood education matters, it is tempting to argue that admissions should open schools in well-educated neighbourhoods to children from elsewhere, so that more disadvantaged pupils share in it. The published data do not support that argument.
The term measures families, not the place. It sits on top of each school’s own prior attainment and disadvantage, so it is not the brighter children a school admits. It fits best at about the scale of a secondary catchment, and it is weaker for faith schools, which recruit less by distance (the review). It describes the families around a school, who are, under catchment admissions, the families whose children attend it. Admitting children from elsewhere changes who the pupils are, not what the school does for them.
It is worth little to disadvantaged pupils. A standard deviation of neighbourhood education is worth +0.8% of Attainment 8 for disadvantaged pupils, about 0.3 points, against +2.6% (about 1.3 points) for non-disadvantaged pupils.
Schools in more educated neighbourhoods have wider gaps, not narrower. Outside London, the gap between non-disadvantaged and disadvantaged pupils’ Attainment 8 rises from 10.9 points in the least educated fifth of neighbourhoods to 14.9 in the most. Holding prior attainment, disadvantage and absence fixed, each standard deviation of neighbourhood education widens it by 1.0 points (t = 11).
Disadvantaged pupils’ value added does not rise with the school’s neighbourhood. Across England the two correlate at 0.12, but that is London, which makes up 49% of the most educated fifth of neighbourhoods and where disadvantaged pupils do unusually well. Outside London the correlation is -0.05, and within local authorities -0.02.
Nor do disadvantaged pupils do better among fewer disadvantaged peers. Given their prior attainment, they do slightly better where more of their schoolmates are disadvantaged: the disadvantage term in their model has an elasticity of +0.027 (t = 7.0).
And Brighton and Hove already runs catchments with random allocation. Its schools are relatively mixed, and adding local segregation to the model changes the authority’s effect not at all (+3.7% against +3.7%).
In one line: neighbourhood education measures the families a school serves, not something the building confers; outside London, disadvantaged pupils at schools in educated neighbourhoods add no more value and face wider gaps. Two cautions. This is school-level evidence, which can show what schools look like but cannot isolate what one pupil would gain by moving, so it does not settle questions of peer effects. And the disadvantaged pupils who attend schools in advantaged neighbourhoods now need not be like those who would under different rules.


So what is it?
The data are school-level, so they cannot settle this. Four readings fit what is above, and they are not exclusive.

Family resources that keep learning going. A day off costs less when someone at home can help catch up: parents with degrees, flexible or home-based work, tutoring, books. FSM does not see this, and neither, quite, does neighbourhood education, which already takes about 32% of the effect and can take no more however it is drawn (above). It counts every adult, not parents. The effect is largest for boys and non-disadvantaged pupils (3rd of 151–152 for both). It is also present for disadvantaged pupils (16th), which fits a city with many lower-income households that are highly educated.
Absence as a stand-in. Across England, high absence travels with things the model does not measure: family stress, poverty beyond FSM, disengagement. Part of the absence coefficient is those things, not the days missed. Where absence comes from somewhere else, the model over-predicts its cost. In Brighton and Hove it is mostly authorised illness, which may include anxiety and other health-related absence that follows a different pattern from disengagement. On this reading the authority effect is partly an artefact of how v2.1 treats absence, not something the schools do.
Recording. Schools and authorities differ in when they authorise illness and how they code it. A practice that authorises more parent-reported illness raises recorded absence without changing learning. This would show up as exactly this pattern, and school-level data cannot tell it from reading 2.
Something the schools or the system do. The 11–16 structure, where entry to the city’s sixth-form colleges depends on GCSE grades, explains a little. Mixed intakes explain nothing measurable. Whatever is left after absence (+0.6%, ranked 59th) is ordinary.



What would help tell them apart
All of these are published:

Absence by pupil characteristics, by authority (DfE, Pupil absence in schools in England). Is the city’s extra absence among pupils eligible for free school meals or not, and in which year groups? Reading 1 predicts it is mostly among the non-disadvantaged.
Census 2021 qualifications for parents rather than all adults: households with dependent children by the household reference person’s qualification or NS-SeC, for school neighbourhoods. This would test reading 1 directly, and would improve v2.1’s neighbourhood term everywhere students and young graduates are concentrated.
Persistent absence and absence reasons by authority over time, against attainment. Reading 3 predicts the city’s illness authorisation sits apart from its neighbours’ with no matching change in attainment.
Elective home education and children missing education (DfE, by authority). These show whether pupils leave school rolls before Year 11 at unusual rates, which would change who sits GCSEs.
Attainment by prior-attainment band in the KS4 performance tables: whether the effect sits with high, middle or low prior attainers.



What it means for v2.1
v2.1 took the 11–16 flag into the expectation: it is a school’s structure, like its admissions policy. It treats a day of absence the same whatever its cause. Adding the illness share of absence improves the fit (AIC -34) and barely changes other authorities’ effects (correlation 0.997), but whether an absence is authorised as illness is partly the school’s own coding, so it stays out of the headline. Value added allowing for the kind of absence is published beside it instead (the methodology). Neither removes Brighton and Hove’s effect. Until the questions above are answered, read the city’s authority effect this way: its schools achieve as much as similar schools elsewhere despite unusually high, mostly illness, absence. It is not evidence that the city’s schools add more than others. With no allowance for absence, the city’s schools average -0.7 points of value added, 102nd of 151 authorities.
The models are in R/06_bh_effect.R.

The national page sets out what the school’s part in absence is. In short:

Who runs a school, its size and its religious character make little difference to absence once intake is allowed for.
Schools with the same intake can differ a great deal, and the differences persist from year to year.

The table compares each of Sussex’s schools with similar schools in its own authority, in 2024/25 and 2025/26. Click a school to open it in Find a twin, which finds its look-alikes across England, and the look-alikes that do much better.

10 schools have unauthorised absence more than 20% below similar schools in both years. What they do may be worth sharing.

title: Explore by area
text:
Every state-funded mainstream secondary school in England has a Value Added v2.1 figure for all pupils, disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils, girls and boys, 2021/22 to 2024/25: Attainment 8 points against England, shrunk by reliability. Choose a level and an area; the map zooms to its schools, a chart shows how each school’s value added has moved year by year, and the table lists them. Click a column heading to sort. “Absence against intake” is percentage points above (positive) or below what the school’s intake predicts.
Colour by offers the same measures as the Sussex pages, for every school in England: value added in each of its forms, attendance (absence, persistent absence, illness, unauthorised absence, reduced timetables, suspensions), results, intake, and the school itself (who runs it, Ofsted, religious character). Value added and absence against intake are coloured on fixed national scales; the other measures run across the range within the chosen area; a measure that is neither better nor worse high or low (disadvantage, EAL, SEN) is shaded in greys. Whichever measure is chosen gets a column in the table.
Period switches between the four-year figure (shrunk, with 95% intervals) and a moving average of the yearly figures, centred on the year you choose, over one, three or five years. A window that runs off the end of the series uses the years there are: a three-year average centred on 2021/22 averages 2021/22 and 2022/23. Yearly figures are not shrunk, so a single year moves more than the four-year figure; see value added over time.






Warning2025/26 is provisional



The last year in the trajectories, and any moving average whose window includes it: 2025/26 is provisional: predicted from the v2.1 model using DfE’s provisional KS4 results (October 2026), with absence bridged from autumn and spring and the intake data not yet published carried forward. It will be updated with the revised KS4 release in February 2027.








Combined and mayoral authorities are from the ONS lookup of local authority districts to combined authorities (May 2025), with the six Devolution Priority Programme areas announced in February 2025 added and marked “(new)”. Areas not in a combined authority are not listed at that level. The full data are in va_v2_schools.csv, and the Sussex areas have pages of their own.

title: How much does a school add? And how much does absence (or anything else) take away?
text: Value Added v2.1 measures each secondary school in England against what its intake and context would lead us to expect: for all pupils, for disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils, and now for girls and boys. It is the next step from How to Pull the Right Lever, rebuilt on the recommendations of a review of the original measure.

title: How much does a school add? And how much does absence (or anything else) take away?
section: What a school adds, and what absence takes away
text:
What a school adds, and what absence takes away
Value added measures what a school does after its intake and context are accounted for, absence included. So the two quantities below are not the same thing counted twice: one is what absence moves, the other is what the school moves once absence has already been allowed for.








Figure 1: An average school, then the same school with absence where the highest 5% of schools sit (full-year absence in 2024/25, 13.0% against a median of 8.4%), then that school doing everything a school can do (value added 2021/22 to 2024/25). Blue is what absence takes away, purple what the school adds back. Attainment 8 points; the dashed line is the England average of 47.5.





Read it left to right. An average school sits at the England mean. Put its absence where the highest 5% of schools sit (13.0% full-year absence in 2024/25, against a typical 8.4%) and it loses 4.6 Attainment 8 points. Now ask it to do everything a school can do – to be a top-ten-per-cent school on value added, net of its intake – and it gains 3.2 back. It is still 1.3 points below where it started. Being exceptional buys back about 71% of what high absence costs.
It also falls hardest on the pupils with the least room to absorb it. The same change in absence is worth 5.1 points of disadvantaged pupils’ Attainment 8, against 3.9 for non-disadvantaged pupils (4.6 for pupils as a whole), and from a lower base: it takes 13.2% of what they would otherwise score rather than 7.7%, a gradient 77% steeper than for non-disadvantaged pupils. Absence is not only the largest lever, it is a regressive one.
One caveat, stated plainly because the scale of this invites over-reading. The model is associational. The gradient says what schools with more absence look like once intake is accounted for, not what a particular school would gain by cutting absence by a given amount. The direction and the order of magnitude are what to take from it. How each number is computed from the model is set out in the methodology.

title: How much does a school add? And how much does absence (or anything else) take away?
text:
What is new since v1

v2.1: schools that stop at 16 are compared with schools like them. An 11–16 school scores a little higher than a similar school with a sixth form; that is its structure, like its admissions policy, so it is now in the expectation.
The kind of absence. Value added allowing for how much of a school’s absence is illness is published beside the headline, on every map (why it is not the headline).
Measured against intake and context only. The Ofsted grade and the teacher workforce terms are out of the expectation: they partly reflect the very performance being measured.
Fairer to schools with harder intakes. Pupil mobility, SEN rates, a single-sex term and neighbourhood education are in.
Against England. A school is compared with similar schools anywhere, with the local authority’s own effect reported beside it.
Honest about uncertainty. Estimates are shrunk by their reliability and carry 95% intervals.
Girls and boys have their own value added for the first time.
The latest Ofsted judgement sits beside every school, including the new report cards.
Over time. Every school has a figure for each year, so trajectories and moving averages over a chosen window sit beside the four-year figure.

title: Methodology – Value Added v2.1
text:
NoteIn one line



Value added v2.1 is each school’s Attainment 8 above or below what a multilevel model expects from its intake and context, measured against England, for five groups of pupils, 2021/22 to 2024/25.

title: Methodology – Value Added v2.1
text:
What matters most
Two ways of asking which terms matter most, side by side. Strength and direction is each term’s effect on expected Attainment 8: for a measure, a move of one standard deviation across England’s schools; for a yes-or-no, the difference between yes and no. Green raises attainment, purple lowers it, and the bars are 95% intervals. Importance splits the variation in Attainment 8 the intake terms explain between them by a Shapley decomposition: each term’s average gain in explained variance over every order in which the terms could be added, so variation two terms share (prior attainment, absence and disadvantage share a great deal) is credited fairly between them rather than to whichever comes first. It is computed by ordinary least squares with the year in every model; the intake terms explain 82% of the variation in log Attainment 8 beyond the year.

All pupilsDisadvantaged pupilsNon-disadvantaged pupils










Figure 1: Strength and direction, all pupils: each term’s effect on expected Attainment 8 in Value Added v2.1, with its 95% interval.













Figure 2: Importance, all pupils: each term’s Shapley share of the variation in Attainment 8 the intake explains.















Figure 3: Strength and direction, disadvantaged pupils: each term’s effect on expected Attainment 8 in Value Added v2.1, with its 95% interval.













Figure 4: Importance, disadvantaged pupils: each term’s Shapley share of the variation in Attainment 8 the intake explains.















Figure 5: Strength and direction, non-disadvantaged pupils: each term’s effect on expected Attainment 8 in Value Added v2.1, with its 95% interval.













Figure 6: Importance, non-disadvantaged pupils: each term’s Shapley share of the variation in Attainment 8 the intake explains.








Prior attainment and absence lead on both counts: 26% and 24% of what the intake explains for all pupils, then disadvantage at 14%. For disadvantaged pupils absence comes first. The two views can disagree, and the difference is worth reading: a term with a large effect but little spread across schools (single-sex schools) explains little variation, and one that moves with others shares its credit. Neither is a causal ranking.

section: The full v2.1 specification, group by group
text:
The full v2.1 specification, group by group
For school \(i\) in local authority \(l\), region \(r\) and year \(t\), and for each pupil group \(g\) (all, disadvantaged, non-disadvantaged, girls, boys) separately:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log(\text{Att8}^{g}_{it}) = \;& \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(\text{FSM6}_{it}) + \beta_2 \log(\text{absence}_{it}) + \beta_3 \log(\text{EAL}_{it}) + \beta_4\, \text{KS2}_{it} \\
&+ \beta_5\, \text{selective}_{i} + \beta_6\, \text{non-selective elsewhere}_{i} + \beta_7\, \text{neighbourhood}_{i} \\
&+ \beta_8\, \text{SEN support}_{it} + \beta_9\, \text{EHCP}_{it} + \beta_{10}\, \text{mobility}_{it} + \beta_{11}\, \text{single-sex}_{i} + \beta_{12}\, \text{11--16}_{i} \\
&+ u_t + v_r + w_{l(r)} + e_{it}
\end{aligned}
\]
\[u_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\text{year}), \quad v_r \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\text{region}), \quad w_{l(r)} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\text{LA}), \quad e_{it} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]
FSM6 is the share of the KS4 cohort disadvantaged; absence the overall absence rate; EAL the share with English as an additional language; KS2 the cohort’s mean KS2 scaled score less 100; admissions are relative to a non-selective school in a highly selective area; neighbourhood is the share of adults qualified to level 4+ in the 150 nearest Census output areas, standardised; SEN support, EHCP and mobility are percentages of pupils; single-sex is a girls’ school (for boys, a boys’ school); 11–16 is a school that stops at 16. Local authorities are nested in regions. Fitted by restricted maximum likelihood in lme4 (R/02_fit_va.R); log-likelihood, AIC and BIC are from the maximum-likelihood refit. R² is Nakagawa’s: marginal for the fixed effects alone, conditional with the random effects too.

title: Methodology – Value Added v2.1
section: What is Bayesian here, and what is not
text:
What is Bayesian here, and what is not
\(\lambda\bar r\) is exactly the posterior mean of a school’s effect under a normal prior centred on zero with variance \(\tau^2\). The arithmetic is Bayesian; the prior is not chosen. \(\tau^2\) and \(\sigma^2\) are estimated by REML from the same data the shrinkage is then applied to, which makes this empirical Bayes rather than Bayes. There is no hyperprior, no sampling and nothing to converge: the posterior is Gaussian and closed form.
The price is that the intervals treat \(\tau^2\) and \(\sigma^2\) as known. They carry the uncertainty in a school’s own mean, not the uncertainty in the variances used to shrink it, so they are a little tighter than a fully Bayesian treatment would give — most so for the groups with the fewest schools.

title: Methodology – Value Added v2.1
section: Two variances, because there are two questions
text:
Two variances, because there are two questions
Against England, a school is credited with everything that separates it from the national picture, its authority and its region included. The prior variance for that comparison is therefore all three persistent components together:
\[\tau^2_\text{England} = \tau^2_\text{school} + \tau^2_\text{LA} + \tau^2_\text{region}\]
Within the authority, the authority and region effects are already in the prediction and are not the school’s to own, so the prior variance is the school component alone. The national figure is the less shrunk of the two: there is more real variation there for it to be variation of. For all pupils that is \(\tau_\text{England} =
0.064\) against \(\tau_\text{school} = 0.059\) on the log scale.

title: Methodology – Value Added v2.1
text:
Back to Attainment 8 points
Shrinkage happens on the log scale, where the model is additive. The shrunken effect is converted against the school’s own mean expected Attainment 8:
\[\text{value added} = \text{base}\left(e^{\lambda\bar r} - 1\right)\]
and its 95% interval the same way, from \(\lambda\bar r \pm
1.96\sqrt{\lambda\sigma^2/n}\). A school counts as significant where that interval excludes zero.
This is a different quantity from the plain four-year mean sitting beside it in the tables: that one averages observed minus expected in points, while this one shrinks a mean log residual and then converts it. For most schools the two are close. For schools with short records or unusual intakes they are not, and the shrunken figure is the one to read.

title: The Value-Added Review
text:
WarningWhere this led



Every recommendation below has been adopted in Value Added v2.0. This page is the review as written, with its figures recomputed from the same analysis (R/21_value_added_review.R in the original repository).
A review of the value-added measure used across the How to Pull the Right Lever work and the Sussex documents. Every figure comes from refitting the published national model on its own data, 12,195 school-years for 3,300 schools, 2021/22 to 2024/25. Nothing uses pupil-level records.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: Why a drop in AIC, and not a Shapley decomposition
text:
Why a drop in AIC, and not a Shapley decomposition
The original lever work decomposed Attainment 8 with Shapley values – the LMG decomposition, which averages each term’s contribution over every order in which the terms could have entered. The table above looks like the same exercise. It is not, and the difference changes how the table should be read.
Dropping a term from the full model measures what that term explains that nothing else does. It is the “added last” extreme: a term is credited with none of the variation it shares with its neighbours. Shapley averages over all orders of entry, so each term is credited with the shared variation exactly as often as it is denied it. The two agree only when the terms are uncorrelated, and these terms are emphatically not: prior attainment, absence and disadvantage all describe overlapping things about the same intake.
The clearest evidence is in the table itself. Disadvantage comes fifth on AIC, below both the Ofsted grade and the local authority, which reads as though how poor a school’s intake is matters less to attainment than its inspection grade. It does not. It means that with prior attainment and absence already in the model there is little left for disadvantage to explain on its own – those two have absorbed most of it. A Shapley decomposition would hand that shared variation back and disadvantage would rise sharply. The bullet above is the same point stated as a finding; it is better understood as a property of the measure.
So the two answer different questions, and neither is the better tool in general:

A drop in AIC asks whether a term earns its place in the model. That is a specification question, and it is the one this document is asking. The penalty means a term has to buy its parameter, and a term that cannot – segregation here – is one the published measure should not be carrying.
A Shapley decomposition asks how to divide the credit between terms that are already in. That is an attribution question, and it was the right one for the lever work, which had to say how much of a gap each driver accounted for. It is also far more expensive: every subset of the terms has to be fitted, against one refit per term here.

Read the table, then, as what it is: how much each term carries that no other term does, beside how far the answer moves without it. For practical purposes the second column is the one to lean on, because it says how many schools actually change quintile rather than how much likelihood is lost. Neither column is a statement about how much each thing matters to a child’s results, and the AIC column in particular should not be quoted as a ranking of importance.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: Things schools partly control: workforce and Ofsted
text:
Things schools partly control: workforce and Ofsted
The workforce terms. Retention, leadership pay and sickness absence are shaped by a school’s leadership as well as by its circumstances. In the baseline, a school that keeps its teachers is expected to do better, so the credit for doing so is netted off its value added. Dropping all three moves 19% of schools a quintile for all pupils, nearly all of it retention, and 7% for disadvantaged pupils. The fit loss is small (AIC 168).
The Ofsted grade. This is the more serious problem. Ofsted’s judgements draw on a school’s results, so putting the grade in the expectation partly conditions value added on its own outcome. An Outstanding school’s bar is raised (the grade’s random effect has a standard deviation of 4.2%), and some of its added value disappears into it. Removing the grade:

moves 34% of schools a quintile (26% for disadvantaged pupils);
changes value added by 0.7 points on average, and by more than 1.6 for one school in ten;
raises the fixed effects’ share of variance (marginal R² from 0.65 to 0.71), because the intake terms take back what the grade had absorbed.

The grade was useful for the Lever report’s purpose, which was to explain attainment. It is the wrong thing to hold constant when the aim is to measure a school against its intake.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: Intake the model misses: mobility, gender, SEN
text:
Intake the model misses: mobility, gender, SEN

Mobility is the best single addition: AIC -293 for all pupils and -241 for disadvantaged. Each extra percentage point of mobile pupils costs 0.5% of Attainment 8. It moves 15% of schools.
Gender. A girls’ school scores +5.4% above an otherwise identical mixed school (boys’ schools do not differ, at -0.1%). A single-sex flag (AIC -191) fits better than the share of girls as a continuous term (AIC -178): the effect is a girls’-school effect, not a gradient across mixed schools.
SEN. SEN support and EHCP rates improve the fit modestly for all pupils (AIC -99) and more clearly for disadvantaged pupils (-93), and move few schools. They belong in the expectation on principle: a school’s SEN intake is not of its making.

title: The Value-Added Review
text:
Neighbourhood education
The preliminary work (Analysis F in the model experiments) found that the share of adults with degree-level qualifications in the 150 census output areas nearest a school, about a 2.5 km radius, improved the model and explained part of the local authority effect. In this review’s terms:

For all pupils it is a strong addition: AIC -239, and one standard deviation of neighbourhood education is worth +2.2%. The local authority standard deviation falls from 0.0262 to 0.0219: it accounts for 30% of the authority variance. Brighton and Hove’s effect falls from +4.5% (5th) to +2.9% (10th). Part of what looked like a Brighton and Hove effect is the city’s educated neighbourhoods.
For disadvantaged pupils it does nothing (AIC +1.4, effect +0.1%). Brighton and Hove’s rank barely moves, from 14th to 15th. Living near educated households does not raise disadvantaged pupils’ results; it is non-disadvantaged pupils, many of whose parents are those households, who carry the effect.

That pattern is what one would expect if neighbourhood education stands in for parental education, which no school-level source measures directly. On that reading it is intake, and belongs in the expectation. Two cautions:

it describes the area around the school, not where its pupils live, so schools with wide or unusual catchments are measured imperfectly;
it is fixed at the 2021 Census, so it cannot track change.


How the neighbourhood is drawn, and why 150
This is the part of v2.0 with no counterpart in the published measure, so it is worth setting out plainly rather than leaving in a citation.
For each school we take its coordinates from GIAS, find the 150 nearest 2021 Census Output Area population-weighted centroids – an exact kd-tree search on the British National Grid, so the distances are metres on the ground and not degrees – and average the census indicators over those output areas. An output area holds about 125 households, so 150 of them is on the order of nineteen thousand: a slice of a town, rather than a street or a region. The indicator the model carries is the share of adults qualified to level 4 or above. Unemployment and economic inactivity were built the same way and are strongly collinear with it, which is why only one of the three is in the specification.
150 was not picked for roundness. The preliminary work built the same variables at k = 10, 25, 50, 100 and 150 and let the fit choose. AIC falls steadily as k grows, bottoms out around 150, and then plateaus and slightly reverses. That shape matters: a variable drifting toward a regional average would keep on improving the fit as the window widened, so a genuine minimum is evidence that 150 is picking up something local rather than washing out into region. Primary schools, run the same way in earlier work, prefer k = 10.
That contrast is the real finding. k is a scale parameter, and the fit recovers catchment geography from the data: secondaries draw from much further than primaries, and the model knows it without being told. At k = 150 the mean radius is about 2.5 km.
There is also a falsification check, which is what makes this more than curve fitting. If the term captures the neighbourhood a school actually serves, rather than generic regional conditions, it should be weaker for schools with a religious character, whose admission is less distance-based by construction. The interaction carries the predicted negative sign, but is not conventionally significant: directionally supportive, underpowered.








Figure 4: One school’s neighbourhood: Dorothy Stringer School (pink) and the 150 nearest 2021 Census output-area population-weighted centroids (purple), with the extent they cover shaded. These are the output areas the neighbourhood term averages over. Hover a centroid for its distance from the school.




For this school the 150th output area is 1.7 km away and the mean is 1.1 km – a compact, genuinely local patch. The same 150 output areas around a rural school would sprawl much further, which is the honest limitation of a fixed k: it is a constant number of households, not a constant distance, so it adapts to population density rather than to how far a particular school’s pupils travel.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: Who runs the school: route and trusts
text:
Who runs the school: route and trusts
Converter academies score +0.9% against maintained schools, free schools, UTCs and studio schools -2.2%, and sponsor-led academies +0.2%. Schools in a multi-academy trust score +1.1%. None of this moves value added much (correlations 0.99 and 1.00).
More importantly, governance should not be in the expectation at all. Who runs a school is one of the things value added is meant to reveal: a trust that improves its schools should see that in their value added, not have it netted off. The worry about selection, that trusts take on schools in difficult circumstances, is met by measuring those circumstances directly (disadvantage, prior attainment, mobility, SEN), not by adjusting for governance. The trust analysis in the East Sussex document is the right place for the governance question.

title: The Value-Added Review
text:
Size and religious character
School size improves the fit for all pupils (AIC -99) but should stay out: popular, successful schools grow, so size is partly a consequence of value added. Religious character makes no difference (AIC +1.9).

title: The Value-Added Review
text:
Absence
Absence is the model’s second most important term. Dropping it moves 45% of schools a quintile, and Brighton and Hove’s authority effect from 5th in England to 30th. It is partly intake (illness, deprivation) and partly practice. The Lever report’s argument rests on keeping it in, and the joint-signal plane already shows the other view, value added with attendance counted in. That pairing is the right answer and needs no change: keep absence in the core measure, and keep publishing the attendance-counted-in version beside it.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: Against the authority, or against England
text:
Against the authority, or against England
The published value added includes the local authority’s random effect in the expectation. With ten or twenty schools in an authority, that effect is largely the average of those schools’ own results, so part of each school’s added value is attributed to its authority and netted off. Measuring against England instead (leaving the authority and region effects out of the prediction):

correlates 0.91 with the published value added across schools, and moves 41% of schools a quintile (42% for disadvantaged pupils);
shifts every school in an authority by the same amount, so it changes comparisons between authorities, not within them.









Figure 5: Each school’s published value added (within its local authority) against its value added measured against England, all pupils, mean 2021/22 to 2024/25. Sussex schools coloured by authority.





Both views are legitimate, but they answer different questions:

Within the authority: “how does this school do compared with similar schools in the same place?”
Against England: “how does this school do compared with similar schools anywhere?”

For the Sussex documents, which compare schools across three authorities, the national version is the right one, and the authority effect should be reported beside it rather than inside it.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: How much of value added is the school
text:
How much of value added is the school
A version of the published model with a school random intercept splits the unexplained variation into a persistent school part and year-to-year noise:

All pupils: the school part has a standard deviation of 0.074 (log scale) against 0.057 for the year-to-year noise. 63% of the unexplained variation is persistent. A four-year average has a reliability of 0.85.
Disadvantaged pupils: 37% persistent, and a four-year average reliability of 0.67. The groups are small, and single years are noisy.

The shrunken school effects from that model correlate 0.90 with the averaged residuals for all pupils, and 0.96 for disadvantaged pupils. The simple average is a good approximation. The shrunken estimate is better for small schools and should be preferred where single schools are singled out.

title: Geographical effects across England
text:
ImportantIn short




Place matters, but less than the school. Once v2.1 has allowed for intake, a local authority one standard deviation above average adds about 2.5% to its schools’ Attainment 8, and a region about 1.5%. A school’s own lasting effect is about 6.0%.
Place matters most for disadvantaged pupils. For them the authority effect is 3.8% and the region effect 2.7%, against 2.4% and 1.6% for non-disadvantaged pupils. Disadvantaged pupils in London do 5.1% better than similar pupils across England; in the South East, 4.1% worse. London’s non-disadvantaged pupils do 1.5% worse.
What goes with it is partly the kind of place, partly the pupils. Disadvantaged pupils do better where schools serve multicultural, urban neighbourhoods. They do worse in small-town, coastal and former industrial areas (Neighbourhood types). Much of that is who the pupils are, since v2.1 has no pupil ethnicity. Some is deprivation that the qualification term misses (Neighbourhood covariates). Most of the authority effects remain unexplained.

title: Geographical effects across England
text:
How much is place?
Value Added v2.1 fits each school’s results with random effects for its region and its local authority. These pick up what places have in common once intake is allowed for. Their size, against each school’s own lasting effect:








Figure 1: How much Attainment 8 varies, once v2.1 has allowed for intake: one standard deviation of the region, local authority and school (lasting) effects, as % of Attainment 8, by group of pupils.





Between the authorities a tenth of the way from the top and a tenth of the way from the bottom, the gap is about 5.7% of Attainment 8 for all pupils (about 2.7 points at the national average), 8.0% for disadvantaged pupils and 5.6% for non-disadvantaged pupils. That is the difference a place makes to otherwise similar schools.
This is why Value Added v2.1 is published two ways. Against England keeps the place in: a school in an authority where similar schools do well looks better. Within the authority takes it out, and compares a school with similar schools nearby.

title: Geographical effects across England
text:
The map
Each authority is coloured by its effect in Value Added v2.1: how far its schools’ results sit from what their intake predicts, as a percentage of Attainment 8, net of its region. Green is above what intake predicts (a positive effect); purple is below (a negative effect). Pale areas are close to zero. These are the same colours as the explorer. Hover over an authority for its figure, interval and rank.

All pupilsDisadvantaged pupilsNon-disadvantaged pupils



































Figure 2: Average value added against England by region (schools’ average log residual, weighted by years, as %): all, disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils. This includes the region’s and its authorities’ effects.





The regional pattern is different for disadvantaged pupils. For all pupils, the South West and North East do best, the North West worst. Non-disadvantaged pupils are similar, with the North East first. For disadvantaged pupils, London leads at +5.1%, and the South East is last at -4.1%. London’s lead belongs to its disadvantaged pupils alone: its non-disadvantaged pupils are at -1.5%. Brighton and Hove’s effect is among the largest in England: +3.8% for all pupils (6th of 152), +3.9% for disadvantaged pupils (18th of 151) and +3.8% for non-disadvantaged pupils (4th of 151). Its own page examines it.

title: Geographical effects across England
text:
What goes with place
What the evidence on this site says about why places differ:

The kind of neighbourhood. The Output Area Classification adds nothing to results within an authority. Between authorities it describes the pattern for disadvantaged pupils. They do better where schools serve multicultural neighbourhoods: group 4c, Challenged Multicultural Communities, has a correlation of +0.34 with the authority effect. They do worse among the classification’s “Baseline UK” neighbourhoods (-0.28) and among small-town (-0.23) and coastal and former industrial ones (-0.20). This is the pattern behind London’s lead and the South East’s position for disadvantaged pupils. For non-disadvantaged pupils the same correlations are much weaker (4c +0.10, 6b -0.12).
Not adult qualifications. v2.1 already allows for neighbourhood education, and the place pattern survives it. Two places with the same share of graduates can differ in diversity, migration and the character of their towns.
Not absence, much. Absence is in the model, and authorities’ absence effects barely track their value added effects: no correlation reaches 0.2 for any of the three groups. For all pupils the largest link is with illness absence, +0.14: where pupils are recorded ill more often than intake predicts, value added is slightly higher. It is the same for disadvantaged pupils (+0.14) but not for non-disadvantaged pupils (+0.02). Brighton and Hove is the clearest case (see What goes with school absence).
A worked example. Brighton and Hove tests the explanations one at a time for one authority.
Who the pupils are, and deprivation the qualification term misses. The neighbourhood covariates experiment added ten Census measures, and each school’s own share of White British pupils, to the model. For disadvantaged pupils, the school’s composition and neighbourhood deprivation together take about a fifth off the authority effects and over a third off the regional ones. The ethnic pattern is mostly the pupils themselves, not the place. For all and non-disadvantaged pupils, authority effects move much less.

title: Geographical effects across England
text:
How far from school?
Where schools are is part of geography too. Across England, children in deprived neighbourhoods usually live closer to a secondary school. In Brighton and Hove they live about a third further away than their neighbours. Absence goes with distance in every year tested, more for disadvantaged pupils, though most of the size of that link between authorities is who lives where, and a smaller link remains. Distance to school sets out the tests, in straight lines.

title: Geographical effects across England
text:
What it means

Read value added against England with the place in mind. Part of a school’s figure is where it is: up to a few per cent for all and non-disadvantaged pupils, more for disadvantaged pupils. The within-authority figure takes that out.
Place effects are largest for the pupils policy most wants to help. A disadvantaged pupil’s results depend more on the authority and region than a non-disadvantaged pupil’s do, even with the same intake.
Part of the place effect is the pupils. v2.1 has no measure of pupils’ ethnicity. The experiment suggests that is much of what makes disadvantaged pupils’ results look like a place effect. The rest of the authority effects are not in the Census at all.

Built by R/12_geography.R from the v2.1 model (R/02_fit_va.R), with boundaries from ONS (counties and unitary authorities, December 2023).

For all pupils the effects are small: about one per cent per standard deviation, or a little more. For disadvantaged pupils they are three to five times larger. Disadvantaged pupils do better around schools in diverse, migrant, less English-speaking and more deprived neighbourhoods, and worse in White British and professional ones. The school’s own White British share is the strongest single term: -5.4% for disadvantaged pupils and -1.5% for all.
For non-disadvantaged pupils the ethnic and migration measures are close to zero: -0.3% for the school’s own White British share and +0.2% for the neighbourhood’s. So what shows up on those measures for all pupils comes mostly from the disadvantaged pupils among them. Deprivation is different. It is as strong for non-disadvantaged pupils (+1.0%) as for all pupils (+1.0%).

Two kinds of deprived neighbourhood

Disadvantaged pupils do far better in the first kind, but most of that is who they are.








Figure 2: Average value added against England (% of Attainment 8, with one standard error) by kind of neighbourhood: under v2.1, with the school’s own ethnicity allowed for, and with neighbourhood deprivation too. Top and bottom thirds of schools on neighbourhood deprivation and neighbourhood education.





Under v2.1, disadvantaged pupils in deprived, graduate-rich neighbourhoods are +7.5% above expectation, and in deprived, low-graduate ones +0.2%. The schools in the first group have 13% White British pupils, against 63% in the second. With that allowed for, the lead falls to +2.4%: two-thirds of it is composition. The rest is real but modest.
Non-disadvantaged pupils in the same deprived, graduate-rich neighbourhoods are at -1.3%. All pupils, at +0.2%, mix the two, so the figure for all pupils hides how differently the two groups do in these places.
Does the graduate idea explain the deprivation effect itself? It makes four predictions, and the data support it only in part:







If it is recent graduates, the deprivation effect should…
What the data show




grow with neighbourhood education
No. The interaction is +0.01% for disadvantaged pupils, -0.30% for non-disadvantaged (the wrong way) and -0.10% for all pupils


sit in London and near universities, not in low-graduate places
In part. For disadvantaged pupils it is +1.6% in London and +1.6% near universities, but also +1.1% in low-graduate places. For non-disadvantaged pupils it is largest in low-graduate places (+1.5%). For all pupils it is much the same in all three (+0.9%, +0.6%, +0.6%)


go once early-career measures are in
No. It stays at +1.3% for disadvantaged pupils, rises to +1.7% for non-disadvantaged and is +1.0% for all pupils


be overcrowding, not ill health
In part. Overcrowding is positive for disadvantaged pupils (+1.5%), but so is bad health (+2.3%). For non-disadvantaged pupils overcrowding adds little (+0.3%) and bad health more (+0.9%). For all pupils they are +1.0% and +1.4%



So the small deprivation term is not a recent-graduate effect. It appears in both kinds of place, for reasons this page cannot separate.
But the graduates may matter in a different way. Two results point the same way. In deprived, graduate-rich neighbourhoods, non-disadvantaged pupils do worse than expected (-1.3%). And at the same share of graduates, more young adults go with slightly lower results for every group (-0.8% for all pupils). A likely reading is that many recent graduates are not the pupils’ parents. Neighbourhood education counts every adult, so young and often childless graduates raise it, and v2.1 then expects more of the local schools than their families warrant. The next section tests that directly.

title: Neighbourhood covariates
text:
Parents, not adults
Neighbourhood education counts every adult. Custom Census 2021 tables from ONS allow something closer to the pupils’ families: level 4+ qualifications among adults aged 25 to 64 in households with dependent children, published by MSOA, the finest level available. Limiting the age leaves out 16 to 18 year olds who are themselves dependent children. Each measure is averaged over a school’s same 150 nearest Output Areas, and all adults are rebuilt at MSOA level too, so differences are about who is counted, not the coarser map.
The measure is distorted where the idea says it should be.

Figure 3: The effect of graduates among parents and among adults without dependent children, entered together with the school’s ethnicity, % of Attainment 8 per SD with 95% intervals, for England, outside London and London.






Non-disadvantaged pupils’ results follow graduate parents (+2.2%, t 9.3). Other graduates nearby add nothing clear (+0.3%). This holds inside and outside London. It is what a measure of family background should do.
Disadvantaged pupils do better near graduates who are not parents (+1.7%, t 4.0), and a little worse near graduate parents (-1.1%). That appears in London and outside it, so it is not simply a London effect. It is smaller than it first looks: about 60% of the split goes once the school’s ethnicity is allowed for, and outside London the parents’ side is no longer clear.
All pupils sit between the two (+1.5% for graduate parents, t 6.6; +0.8% for other graduates, t 3.0). They mix two groups that respond in opposite ways to graduate parents.

The second result fits the idea that young graduates bring something to a neighbourhood that reaches disadvantaged pupils. It fits other stories too. Disadvantaged pupils among graduate parents may be more isolated, or more disadvantaged within their school. The two measures also overlap heavily (correlation 0.88), so the split rests on the places where they differ. It is an association to follow up, not a finding about cause.
For the model. Neighbourhood deprivation survives with parents measured properly, so the case for it in v2.2 stands. Splitting neighbourhood education into parents and other adults would help every group a little, and is a further candidate. Parents here means adults aged 25 to 64 in a household with a dependent child, which also takes in some grandparents and older siblings, at MSOA level.

title: Neighbourhood covariates
section: Do they explain the place effects?
text:
Do they explain the place effects?








Figure 4: How much the local authority and region variances change when each set of terms is added (%). Negative: the terms account for part of what the authority or region effects were picking up.





For disadvantaged pupils, the school’s composition with neighbourhood deprivation takes 23% off the local authority variance and 38% off the regional variance. Part of why disadvantaged pupils do better in London and some cities than in the South East or coastal towns is who the pupils are and what their neighbourhoods are like, at the same intake otherwise.
For all pupils, authority effects barely change and regional ones grow. Non-disadvantaged pupils are much the same: the authority variance falls by 9% and the regional variance rises by 15%. The measures account for differences within regions, which leaves the differences between them larger. For most pupils, what makes an authority’s schools do better is not in these measures.

title: Neighbourhood covariates
section: What it means for the model
text:
What it means for the model

A candidate for v2.2: pupils’ ethnicity. DfE’s contextual value added, in the performance tables until 2011, included pupils’ ethnicity. Progress 8 does not, and nor does v2.1. The evidence here is that leaving it out matters most for disadvantaged pupils, and hardly at all for non-disadvantaged pupils. Whether to put it in is a question of what the measure is for. Adjusting for it would stop schools with many White British disadvantaged pupils looking worse for it. It would also take a real difference in results out of view. It belongs with the review’s other recommendations.
A candidate for neighbourhood: deprivation beside education. Adding household deprivation to neighbourhood education improves the model for every group. It is not specific to graduate-rich places (above), and a measure of parents’ qualifications may do the job better.
What is left of place. Even with all of it, most of the local authority effects remain, especially for all and non-disadvantaged pupils. What makes some authorities’ schools do better than their intakes predict is not in the Census.

Each model is the full v2.1 specification for its group, with the same random effects for year and region/local authority, fitted by maximum likelihood so that AIC can be compared. The school’s own White British share is from January 2026 and is used for every year, since earlier school census files in the performance tables do not include ethnicity. title: Value Added v2.2 candidates
section: Who would gain and who would lose
text:
Who would gain and who would lose








Figure 2: The average change in schools’ value added (Attainment 8 points) with both terms added, by fifth of schools on their share of White British pupils, for each group.





With both terms, disadvantaged value added falls by 2.3 points on average in the fifth of schools with the fewest White British pupils (about 13%), and rises by up to 0.7 in the middle and upper fifths. By region, London’s schools lose 2.0 points of disadvantaged value added on average; every other region gains a little, except the West Midlands (-0.4).

title: Value Added v2.2 candidates
section: The case for and against ethnicity
text:
The case for and against ethnicity
For. Value added is meant to compare schools fairly, on what they do rather than whom they teach. Disadvantaged White British pupils do less well wherever they are taught. A school that serves many of them is judged against schools whose disadvantaged pupils were always more likely to do well. Adjusting for it is what DfE’s contextual value added did until 2011. It is also what the evidence here supports, for this group, in every year.
Against. An expectation that varies by ethnicity builds a lower expectation into the measure for some pupils. That was the main criticism of contextual value added and part of why it was dropped. It would also take out of view a real gap that policy should see: the low attainment of disadvantaged White British pupils. And the term is a school share, not each pupil’s own ethnicity, so it adjusts schools, not pupils.
What we would do. Publish it beside v2.2 rather than in it, as v2.1 publishes value added allowing for the kind of absence. The headline measure stays free of ethnicity. Anyone asking “how does this school do with its particular disadvantaged pupils?” can see the answer next to it.

title: Value Added v2.2 candidates
section: What we would recommend for v2.2
text:
What we would recommend for v2.2






Tip



This approach is agreed and on the roadmap for a future release. Until then, everything on this site is Value Added v2.1.



Add neighbourhood deprivation to the expectation, beside neighbourhood education. It is a neighbourhood measure, like the term it sits next to. It helps every group in every year. It is not specific to graduate-rich places (Two kinds of deprived neighbourhood), and it survives with parents’ qualifications measured properly.
Publish value added allowing for pupils’ ethnicity beside the headline, for every group, labelled, with this page as its explanation.
Keep testing: whether the ethnicity effect is a White British effect or varies by group (Gypsy, Roma and Traveller, Black Caribbean and others), using the census’s detailed shares.

title: How school absence changes
text:
NoteWork in progress



This page continues the absence analysis. That page compares different schools in one year. This one follows the same schools over ten years. Every figure comes from published school-level data, so every result is about schools, not pupils.

title: How school absence changes
text:
Why follow schools over time
Comparing schools in one year mixes up two things: what a school’s pupils and community bring, and what the school does. Following the same school over time holds constant everything about it that does not change: its neighbourhood, its buildings, its reputation, most of its intake. What is left is change. So this page asks:

How much of a school’s absence is lasting, and how much moves from year to year?
Do schools keep their place?
Who rose most between before the pandemic and now?
When a school’s own intake changes, does its absence change with it?
What happens to absence when a school becomes an academy, or moves to a new trust?

title: How school absence changes
text:
The data

Absence. DfE’s school-level absence for the autumn and spring terms, 2016/17 to 2025/26. It is the one file that covers every year on the same basis, including 2025/26, whose full-year figures are not published until 2027. 2019/20 was not collected. 2020/21 is shown in the trend but left out of every model: in a year of lockdowns, pupils told to stay home were not counted as absent.
Schools. Every state-funded secondary school: 30,592 school-years, 3,524 schools. A school that becomes an academy, or moves trust, gets a new URN. The 4,271 URNs are joined into schools with GIAS’s one-to-one predecessor and successor links. Mergers, amalgamations and splits end a school’s record.
Intake. The January school census for 2018/19 and 2021/22 to 2024/25 (the performance tables’ census files) and 2025/26 (the January 2026 school census and SEN files). Earlier years are no longer published in the same form.

title: How school absence changes
text:
Ten years of absence








Figure 1: Absence in England’s state-funded secondary schools, autumn and spring terms, indexed to 2018/19 = 100 (sessions-weighted for the reasons; % of pupils for persistent and severe). 2019/20 was not collected; 2020/21 (shaded) was a year of partial closure.





Absence across the autumn and spring terms rose from 5.2% of sessions in 2018/19 to 8.7% in 2022/23. It has eased only to 8.0% in 2025/26. Illness has fallen most of the way back. Unauthorised and other authorised absence have not. Severe absence, pupils missing half their schooling or more, has risen from 1.2% of pupils to 3.6%, and is still near its peak.

title: How school absence changes
section: What stays with a school and what moves
text:
What stays with a school and what moves








Figure 2: Where the variation in each kind of absence lies, once the national year-to-year swing is taken out: multilevel models of log absence with year effects and region, local authority and school random effects, 2016/17 to 2025/26 without 2020/21. ‘Year to year’ is a school’s movement around its own lasting level.






Most absence is lasting. Once the national swing from year to year is taken out, 66% of the variation in overall absence, 69% of unauthorised and 68% of persistent absence is a school’s lasting level. Its region and local authority account for about a tenth; the rest is movement from year to year.
Illness moves more, and is more about place. Only 38% of the variation in illness is lasting to a school, 41% moves from year to year, and 14% is the local authority. That fits the cross-section, where illness was the kind of absence most tied to place.
The national swing is large. Year alone accounts for 38% of all the variation in overall absence over the period, and 31% of severe. Any one school’s change from last year is mostly the country’s change.

title: How school absence changes
text:
Do schools keep their place?








Figure 3: Correlation between years of each school’s absence relative to England that year (log scale), for the schools present in both years. 2020/21 is included here for completeness.





From one year to the next, schools barely move: the correlation of overall absence between 2024/25 and 2025/26 is 0.94. Over longer stretches they do. Between 2018/19, before the pandemic, and 2025/26 the correlation is 0.68 for overall absence, 0.76 for unauthorised and only 0.41 for illness.
Put another way, of the fifth of schools with the highest unauthorised absence before the pandemic (2016/17 to 2018/19), 62% are still in the top fifth now (2023/24 to 2025/26). For overall absence it is 54%. If nothing changed, it would be 20%. If nothing moved, 100%. A school’s place is sticky, but it is not fixed: more than a third of the schools with the most absence before the pandemic no longer have.

The rise was broadly proportional. Schools with the fewest pupils on free school meals saw overall absence rise by 46%. Schools with the most saw 60%. In percentage points, the gap widened: 2.1 points against 3.7.
Unauthorised absence doubled almost everywhere, slightly less in the poorest schools in relative terms (+98% against +121%) but by far more in points.
Severe absence roughly tripled in every fifth, from 0.7% of pupils to 2.2% in the least disadvantaged schools and from 1.6% to 5.0% in the most.
Illness rose least in the poorest schools (+24% against +35% in the second fifth).

So the pandemic did not reorder schools so much as scale them up. A school’s absence now is best compared with where it was relative to England before, not with its own pre-pandemic figure.

title: How school absence changes
section: When a school’s own intake changes
text:
When a school’s own intake changes
The cross-section shows that schools with more pupils on free school meals or SEN support have more absence. That could be because of those pupils, or because of everything else that goes with being that kind of school. Following the same school as its intake changes separates the two. If a school’s absence moves with its own intake, the intake matters directly. If not, the cross-school pattern is mostly about the kind of school and community.








Figure 5: Difference in absence (%) with a change in intake, between schools (pooled, with year effects; pale) and within the same school over time (school and year fixed effects; dark), 2018/19 and 2021/22 to 2025/26, with 95% intervals clustered by school.






Between schools, disadvantage goes with far more unauthorised absence than within one. Across schools, five points more pupils on free school meals goes with +20% unauthorised absence. When one school’s own share rises by as much, its unauthorised absence rises by +5%. Most of the cross-school gradient is about the kind of school and community, not the marginal pupil.
The same holds for SEN support: +10% between schools, +2% within.
For overall absence the two are closer (+5.6% and +3.8% for FSM), so a school taking more disadvantaged pupils should expect somewhat more absence.
Intake change explains little of how a school’s absence moves. The changes in intake account for 4.8% of the within-school variation in overall absence, 2.0% of unauthorised and 2.3% of persistent. Intake does not move much within a school (Table 2), and when absence moves, it is mostly something else.

title: How school absence changes
section: Becoming an academy, or changing trust
text:
Becoming an academy, or changing trust
Two kinds of change give a school a new URN, so they can be dated precisely:

Becoming an academy. 374 maintained schools converted between 2017/18 and 2025/26 and can be followed either side, compared with schools that were maintained throughout and those that had yet to convert.
A change of trust. 155 academies moved to a new trust, compared with academies that stayed put.

Each is an event study (Sun and Abraham’s estimator, with school and year effects): how absence moved, relative to similar schools that did not change, in the years before and after. The years count only the years with data, so the pandemic gap is one step.

Becoming an academy makes no clear difference. In the years after conversion, overall absence was within 0.8% of schools that stayed maintained (95% interval -1.2% to +2.9%). But the converting schools were already on a different path: their absence was rising relative to schools that stayed maintained in the years before, and that rise stopped. So the honest reading is no visible effect of conversion itself, among schools whose trajectory was already diverging.
A change of trust is followed by lower absence. In the years after a move, unauthorised absence was 12% lower and persistent absence 16% lower, relative to academies that stayed with their trust. Overall absence was 6% lower. Three things to weigh:

The schools were getting worse first. Absence rose in the two or three years before the move (persistent absence three years before was 11% lower than in the year before), which is often why a school is moved. Some of the fall is recovery. But persistent and unauthorised absence fell well below where they had been three years before the move.
The pupils did not get easier. The share on free school meals rose by +2.7 points relative to other academies, and the roll changed little.
Recording may change too. A new trust brings new attendance policies, and how sessions are coded is partly a school’s choice. Other authorised absence also fell, so this is not just unauthorised absence being authorised instead.

title: How school absence changes
text:
What it means






TipFor heads and governors




Judge your absence against England’s year, not your own last year. The national swing is the largest single thing in any school’s change from one year to the next.
Compare with where you stood relative to England before the pandemic, not with your pre-pandemic figures. Everyone’s rose, and roughly in proportion.
A school’s absence is mostly lasting, but not fixed. Two-thirds of the variation is a school’s own level, and the same schools tend to stay high. More than a third of the highest-absence schools before the pandemic are no longer in the top fifth.
A change in intake is rarely the reason absence moved. Within a school, changes in its pupils explain only a few per cent of changes in absence.
What happens in the school seems to matter. A change of trust, which usually means new leadership and new attendance policies, is followed by lower unauthorised and persistent absence, even with more disadvantaged pupils. To see who has done it with an intake like yours, Find a twin.



For policy, the same results say that the post-pandemic rise is a national shift, not something concentrated in a few kinds of school, and that structural change (becoming an academy) is not by itself a lever on attendance. What a new trust does might be.

title: How school absence changes
text:
What this cannot tell us

It is about schools, not pupils. A school’s absence can change because its pupils change, or because the same pupils attend differently. Published data cannot tell these apart.
Event studies are not experiments. Schools are moved to a new trust for reasons, often falling standards. The comparison schools did not face the same pressures, and the pre-move rise shows it.
Recording practice varies. Whether a session is coded as illness, authorised or unauthorised is partly a school’s choice, and can change with a new head or trust.
The intake series is short and its FSM measure shifted. Intake by year is available for six years, and eligibility under Universal Credit raised FSM shares in ways that do not all reflect more poverty.
Chains break. A school that merges or splits starts a new record, so the most disrupted schools are under-represented.

title: How school absence changes
text:
Next steps

Each school’s own path, relative to England, on the area pages and in Find a twin’s fact cards.
Illness or recording? Started on What goes with school absence, which finds a partial trade-off between illness and unauthorised absence.
The severe tail, which has tripled and is not falling, on its own.
Trusts. Whether particular trusts’ schools move together after joining, which would point to what the trust does.
Back into value added: absence against intake, by kind, as a candidate for a future version of the model.
